summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs.3,10,623 as the value of all the debts owed by the assessee on the valuation date. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax officer included a sums of Rs,3,20,624 as the net wealth of the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner followed "Commissioner 's decision in Dipti Kumar Basu vs Iysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa) and held that interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that accrued interest was not liable tobe included in wealth tax assessment for the relevant assessment years, 1965 66 67 and 1966 68. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The computation of the net assets of an assessee calls for a determination of his assets and debts as on the date of valuation. All the assets of the assesse are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounting adopted by the assesses. [310 B] (2) In the instant case, the accounts of the respondent assessee were maintained on cash basis. The method of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets and liabilities as on valuation date in terms of the last day of the "previous year" taking into account the financial activities of the assesses during that "previous years". [310 C D] (3) In order to determine the net income of an assesse, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the value date. The system of accountancy, mercantile, cash or Hybrid, is of any relevance for determining the net Wealth Tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts are maintained on a cash basis, although not realised, on thestandings of the money lending business are liable to been included in its net wealth.

The respondent was a civilian employee of the Central Administrative Tribunal. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been convicted by a criminal court for an offence punishable under section 302 IPC and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal, which was allowed by the High Cou rt. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty imposed upon him as he had not been given any opportunity to defend himself and that the punishment of dismissal should be maintained. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of the Tribunal imposing a lesser penalty on the respondent was set aside by the Supreme Court. [534B] 2.2 In the instant case, since the respondent had been acquitted in the criminal case, he could not have been given an opportunity to represent himself before the authorities. He had been given a reasonable opportunity to cross examine the witnesses and to produce documents. The order imposing a penalty on him was not justified by any reason whatsoever. [334C D] 2.(a) In the present case, the respondent has failed in proving that he was not in fact the person convicted. He has been in fact convicted. Therefore, the High court could not interfere with his punishment if the conclusion of the inquiry officer or the Tribunal is based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. [434D] (b) The respondent failed into proving that the charge alone would have weighed with the authority in imposing the penalty. In view of the aforesaid discussion, the order passed by the Tribunal imposed a lesser punishment on the appe lant and the High Cour t was not right in interfering with the order imposing the lesser penalty. [34E F] (c) The High Court has no jurisdiction if the findings of the enquiry officer or Tribunal are based on materials even if any of it was found tobe irrelevant or irrelevant to the mater. [35F G] 2(a) The power under section 25 of the Act is not absolute and unfettered but it is subject to certain limitations. It is a well settled principle that when an authority comes to know that a disciplinary proceeding has been held against him, it must consider whether his conduct which has been found to have been proved or not. If it is so, what penalty should be imposed would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [36F G H] (d) The Court can interfere with an order imposing lesser penalty if the conditions of the provi sion are satisfied. [33G] 3(a). In the light of the principles to which we have call ed attention and in view of this Court in Shankar Dass vs Union of India, ; , it becomes apparent that in the case of transfer proceedings from a civil court or High Court, the Tribunal can exercise all the powers whi ch the civil court could in a suit or the High Commis sioner, as final, and even otherwise dealt with und er the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules which are undispu rised by the authorities in dismissing the public servant. [37F G; 38A] 4(b). The respondent has been dismissed from servi cial service for a long time without any notice or opportunity to him. He is entitled to be reinstated in service with back wages.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for declaration and injunction to restrain the appellants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral dole Predio Aiva Aoiva Aor Predo Aor Aor predo Yeno A or Predu Aor Ror Pedo Ao A.O.A.A., A.A, A.E.A and A.D.A respectively from the date of the suit till the date on which possession was taken by the Civil Court. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not a deemed purchaser of the property in respect of which he claimed to be a lessee. In appeal, the High Court held that the suit was barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and had therefore allowed the first defendant to become a deemed tenant. The High Court dismissed the second appeal filed by the appellants. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 85A which provides that where any person as is referred to in section 4 (deemed tenant) has been evicted from the land on or after 1st July 1962 his remedy under section 8(2) is to approach the authority under the Act for recovery of possession of the land in the manner prescribed by or under the Land Acquisition Act. [1032G] 2.1 The jurisdiction of the Civil Courts stands wholly barred by virtue of Section 58(2). In such a situation the Civil court would not be competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant, because it would not lie in the Civil Judge to give any relief to the landlord by way of possession. [1132G H] 2:1 The civil Court would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant was a deemed landlord of the agricultural land. If the decision of the Mamlatdar is in favour of the party raising the plea, the suit for possession would have to be dismissed, because, it would be just and proper that the issue whether defendant No.1 was a tenant or a deemed tenancy was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar and the jurisdiction of Civil Court precluded from deciding the same in view of section 7 read with section 58(3). [1133A B] 2 :2 The jurisdiction is vested in the Mamlatdar under Section 7 of the Act and had, therefore, allowed the plaintiff to become deemed purchaser. If on the other hand, he is held to be tenant, the Civil suit for eviction would haveto be dismissed because it was not open to the Civil judge to give such relief to a landlord by means of possession or is the jurisdiction conferred upon the Mamlatdar. [1233C D] 3:3 The jurisdiction vested in civil courts stands wholly excluded from deciding whether a person is a deemed tenants or adeemed tenant. If, on the contrary, the landlord proves that the termination of tenancy was in the way authorised by section 9, the civil court would be competent not to pass an order for possession to such deemed tenant.[1233D] 4:4 The jurisdiction conferred on the Mamlatdar by Section 58 (2) of Civil Courts Act is expressly barred by sub section (2). [1234E] 5.1 In a situation where a person who was adeemed landlord under section 4 of the Land Acquiring Act, is evicted from land on the strength of his tenancy, a question whether he was a 'deemed tenant or deemed tenant was requiredto be decided in view thereof and after his decision is received by the civil Court, the jurisdiction is expressly excluded from determining the same. [1334G] 5:5.2 The Civil Court would not have been competent to decide the same on the basis of section 8 read with Section 58 of the Bombay Tenancy Act.

The petitioners are carpenters in Government service. They claim that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work. The Corporation has adopted the minimum wages payable for similar work in the construction industry. The petitioners have been described as daily rated employees. The respondents contended that there were no regular employees of the petitioners ' establishment and, therefore, question of payment of salary admissible to them was not justified. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The principle of equal pay is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. It is important to emphasize that equal pay must depend upon the nature of work done, it cannot be judged by mere volume of work, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. [682B C] 1.2. The principles of equal wages cannot be invoked invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. It will, therefore not be correct to provide two different pay scales in the same establishment on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. [782C D] 1.(a) The principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitution. In the instant case, the petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the . By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter is equal to the other in the performance of his work. [667E] 1(b) The petitioners are engaged by a Company incorporated under section 617 of the Companies Act, 1956 and are being paid the minimum wage payable for identical work. They are being given the same pay as carpenter or craftsmen. The Court while rejecting the claim of the peti tioners, however, cannot direct the Corporation to apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P. 2 unless the Government makes it applicable to employees of Government service, the petitioner cannot enforce the right to "equal pay for Equal work" in every case of similar work. Nor can there be qualitative differences as regards quality and responsibility, nor can deny that sometimes the difference lies as regards value and responsibility.[667E F] 1:2. In view of the fact that equal wages for equal Work is a concomitant of Article 14, it is not possible to provide both different pay scale in the similar establishment and also to popular handicise and trade craftsman. [669G H] 2(a) There are no regular workmen of the petitioner ' establishment or, as such, the question of pay admissible to such workmen. The principal claim of these petitioners is fails and is rejected. [670E F G] 3(b). The principle for equal pay has not been invoked invariably In every case, there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the same master in thesame establishment. It cannot be enforced. [671G H; 669A] 4(c) The principles laid down in Randhir Singh case are not applicable to the petitioners. The petition is dismissed.

The prosecution case against the first accused was that on or about 29.11.1975, at Babultara and Waghala village, all the seven accused persons along with five others committed murder of Malan in furtherance of their common intention they committed the murder of his wife Malan. The Sessions Judge convicted all the accused under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to the first two accused. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the retracted confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against him in view of the fact that he had been acquitted by the High court of Maharashtra. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted confession made by accused 5 to the deceased Malan is admissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act and the same cannot be used against other accused except accused 6. [601 B] 2.1 In order to convict a person for an offence of murder of a person who has been convicted, the court must first consider the evidence adduced by the prosecution in support of the charge and then come to its own conclusion whether the accused had committed the offence. The Court must first examine the evidence on record and then determine whether the conviction was sustainable or not. [701 C] 2:2.1 The retracted confessional statement made by the accused 5 cannot be relied on against him for the purpose of convicting him under section 120B I. P.C., as it is inadmissible in evidence. [700 D] 2(a) In order that the court may examine the entire evidence adduced before it, the Court must consider the circumstances and circumstances of each case. The court must also consider the probabilities of the case. [600 C] (b) The retracted confessions made by an accused 5 are admissible under s.27 of the Indian Evidence Act. [110 D] 3(a). In order whether a retracted confession is admissible, the courts must first take into consideration the circumstances of the particular case and then arrive at its own conclusions on the basis of evidence adduced in that behalf. [1101 B C] 4(b) It is not necessary for the court to consider the entire facts and circumstances in each case as it may be possible to come to a conclusion whether there was sufficient ground for believing the retracted confessions. The courts must also take into account the circumstances which have been brought on record by the defence and the surrounding circumstances. [1001 C D] 5(c) In the instant case, the retracted confessional statements of accused 1 to 4 were not admissible under S.27 I.C.; they were inadmissible in view Of the fact, that accused 6 had been tried alongwith accused 5 for the murder committed by him only against accused 1 and 6. The confession made to accused 5 was inadmissible in law. [1002 D] (d) In view of this Court 's decision in State of Maharashtra vs Ram Gopal, ; , it is not possible to accept the contention that retracted confessions are admissible in evidence under section27 of Evidence Act because they are admissible only under s,27 of Indian Evidence Code.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of a will executed by Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, in favour of the respondent, and after her death, the appellant had executed a will. The question for decision is whether the will set up by him was not proved to be the last will and if so, whether it was true that it was his will in the sense that it represented her intentions. Held, that the testator 's evidence about the execution of the will was highly improbable and the onus was heavy on him to remove the suspicions attending the execution. The fact that he had no clear recollection as to what happened on the day when he attested the will would not make any difference in the case of the appellant. The test for determining whether a will is proved is whether it is true that the will has been executed by the testator at the relevant time and was duly signed; but it cannot be said that the attesting witnesses were not examined to prove the execution, because they had no recollection about the contents of the Will. The onus of proving that the testatrix fully understood the nature and effect of its contents was on the propounder. Held further, that in a case where the testator had executed the will he must have known the provisions of the instrument he had signed it and put his signature to the document before he put her signatures to the will. In such a case the onus of proof would be heavy on the appellant who had failed to discharge the burden. The burden of proving the execution was upon him to show that the Will was not duly executed by him. Held also, further,that the evidence about previous instructions given by Lakshmaamma in favour Of the respondent did not establish that she was in a sound disposing state of mind or that it had been written in one room and Lakshmammal had understood its contents. The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that on proof of the signature of the testatrix, the will had been read out to the testatrix and she understood the effect of the dispositions.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of Arcinema and had been manufacturing Arcocons. The sales tax authorities assessed the goods under section 4(1) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act '). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment but reduced the tax to Rs. 1,00,000/ on the ground that they fall under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Act. The High Court held that such goods were "electrical goods" falling within Entry 41 of Schedule 1 of the Madras General Sales tax Act,1957 and that the appellant company could be covered by the entry under consideration. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the expression "accessories" in Entry No.4 of the First Schedule of 1963 meant only those goods which are ordinarily used for other purposes as well as for use as an aid or addition; and (ii) the word "cinumema" in entry No 4 of Schedule I of the Bombay Sales Tax Rules, 1957 was not "electric goods". Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "all goods" is used in Entry 41 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and the meaning of this entry can only be satisfactorily determined in the light of the language of the entry itself considered in the context in which it occurs. [701C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the expression 'accessories ' is used with reference to parts which are not ordinarily used or for other purpose as well. The word "all" has been used in several entries like that in the schedule relating to "accessory". It would be noticed that the term "accessts" is defined in entry 41 of List II and includes "all articles (including batteries) adapted for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment". [702D E] 2(a) The expression 'electrical articles ' has been employed with reference only to parts. It does not mean that the expression `accessories used in a schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for agricultural purposes merely because some part of a particular kind of apparatus is not necessarily included within the relevant entry. [0702F] 2.(b) The word 'accessory ' has not been defined in the Act and it cannot be said that the word `accessory" used in the Schedule to describe articles which may be manufactured for use or accessories connected with the main purpose of the assessee would not cease to be covered under an entry meant for goods intended for use. [ 702G] 2 (c) The words "parts thereof" are used in various entries like the one relating to items which are generally used for purposes other than as well, and therefore, they cannot detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. [700F G] 3(d) The meaning of the word 'electric articles ' is not merely that part of the earth or permanently fastened to it but also that part thereof which may contain some parts of a kind of instrument of manufacture for use for a particular type of apparatus would not be covered within the entry. The words `accesss ' and `accesstiories ' are used for the purpose of equipment or accessories associated with the Main purpose. [602G H] 4(a). The word `electric article ' has to be understood in its ordinary sense, as meaning a part of an instrument of sale of goods. It is not necessary that the words `as well as 'accesstiory ' should be understood as including parts which may consist of articles which are capable of being used for use by the assessee or for any other purpose. The term `accessible ' has also been defined to include parts which have been used for a specific purpose.

The petitioners in some of the petitions had challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 under section 15 of the (67 of 1957) and the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the said notification was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution inasmuch as it purported to impose royalty on minor minerals which were not specified in the Schedule to the Act. The respondents contended that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to The Gujarat Minor Minerals Rules 1966, the State Government had to pay royalty at the rate of 50 per cent of the rate prescribed for minor minerals and for other purposes sanctioned by law. The contention was that under entry 50 of list II of 7th schedule to the 7 th Schedule to that Act, the royalty recovered by the State government had to be used only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The impugned notification in question was in violation of clause(b) to rule 21 of the Rules. It is no doubt true that the Act is passed for de opment of minerals but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the same tax should be used merely for mineral Development and could be used either for other purpose or for other objects sanctioned by laws. [419C D] 1.2 The Act is enacted for deplo sive purposes of development, including development, where the State otherwise allows mining of minerals to be undertaken in public interest. It does not involve any movement as such. It merely authorises the State to show a concession in the matter of payment of royalty at a rate higher than 50 per percent of the royalty payable by the lessees and no royalty is payable by village potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks and who supply at least one lakh brick and who supplies at least two lakh bricks to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. [416D E] 1.(a) The State incidentally permits mining to the rural Housing Board, if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot be said that there was no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule21 and the social policy underlying the Constitution. [414B C] (b). The word "improvement" in section 15(67) of 1957 means that the State may impose a tax on minor mineral or minerals which are not specified therein. But the word "intermediary" is used in the proviso only for development of minerals and not for other pur pose. [420C] (c) The word 'improject ' has been used in section 2(a)(i) of the Act to mean that no mining lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of specified minor mineral and the area covered by a mining lease is much longer than 10 years in respect of minor minerals except in the case of ordinary sand, Murram and gravel and in the cases of ordinary Sand, Muraram and grale. The word `improtion ' has not been defined in the Act but it has been defined to mean a grant or renewal of a mining licence or any other mineral concession granted under any rule made under any Rule made under sub section (1) of Section 15 of 1957. [406D E; 417A] 2.(a)(ii) The expression "impreference" in the context of the provisions of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948 is not defined in that Act but has been interpreted by this Court in State of Gujarat vs M/s. Ambalal Mills Ltd., ; , followed.

The appellant was the trustee of a temple. The trusteeship of the temple was conferred on the appellant by section 6(9) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1959 (Act 22 of 1959). Under section 6 of the Act, the hereditary trustee is entitled to succession by the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the office as a matter of course. The appellant was appointed as the trusteeship in the temple and he was given a right to manage the temple. He filed a suit for declaration that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6 (9) Of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree holding that the respondent was not hereditary trustee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The definition of hereditary trustee in section 6 is identical in both the Acts. It is now well established that the office of a hereditary trustees is in the nature of property. [446 B] (2) A hereditary trustee has no right to be appointed as a trustee unless he is expressly provided for by the founder himself who created the endowment. The mere fact that the successor owes his title to the appointment or the authority to appoint is vested in the assembly of the bairagis and the worshippets does not affect independent title. [546 C] (3) A religious institution is a hereditary office because its succession depends on the volition of the last incumbent and does not rest upon independent title, but it is for a fixed period of one year and not for life. It was therefore difficult to hold that the appointment of the appellant is hereditary within the definition of section 2(9). [447 D] (4) The artificial definition of 'hereditary trustee in Section 6(1) of Act 19 of 1951 must be construed along with the phrase "succession to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and usage. [427 E] (5) The word 'successor ' in section 2 (9), as used in section 4(9), means a person who is appointed to be hereditary trustee, but does not include such persons.

The appellant was charged with murder under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The prosecution alleged that the deceased was last seen alive on April 26, 1971 at about 10.00 P.M. in the open space of his cattle shed in the north Boothagudi channel. On April 26. 1971 he was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle sheds in the south Bootligudi channel and when he went near his brother who came from the side of the sluice of the north boothagudora channel, he saw that the appellant was sleeping with his brother, who was sleeping at a bench where he was sitting. He ran away after the assault. The deceased chased him and ran away. The appellant was also sleeping on the eastern parapet of the Sluice. On the next day when he was standing near his deceased brother, he was found sleeping on an open space in the front portion of the roof of the shed. When he went to his elder brother who was sitting there, he noticed that the accused had fallen down on the southern side of a sluices of the south bootagudi channel which is shown at No. 1 and he ran away from the place where he fell dead. The police submitted charge sheet under section302/34 IPC against the appellant. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 304 Part II, I.P.C. and sentenced him to death under section 307 read with Section 34 I. P.C., and sentenced each of them to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court had not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW 4 in so far as he implicated the second accused; (ii) the first information report was true that his earlier version in the first Information Report was only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran alias Kanyakumari Comrade alias Ramu and also stated that he was afflicted with the fell disease of leprosy; (iii) the evidence showed that the first informant had stated in the First Information Report that "my elder brother" was "chasing him from behind" in court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has not considered this intrinsic quality as sufficient to base the quality of testimony of PW4. [707C] 2.1 In a case where conviction of the accused depends on the sole testimony of a single witness, it is only necessary that the court should be circumspect and closely scrutinise the evidence to come to an unhesitating conclusion that he is absolutely reliable. The court must be circumspect, carefully scrutinised the evidence and closely scrutinize the evidence. [807D] 2(a) In a criminal case where the conviction of an accused depends solely on the testimony of one single witness. It is only appropriate that the Court should be cautious and closely scrutinised the entire evidence to coming to an irresistible conclusion that the prosecution has made a correct approach in assessing the quality. The mere fact that the witness may not have seen the other assailants who might have already escaped, cannot by itself be a ground for disbelieving the testimony with regard to the assailants. [825E F] 2.(b) In the instant case, the High court was not right even that the evidence was corroborated by the contents of the FIR. The fact that PW 4 had stated that "his elder brother is sitting there" in Court he has completely given a go by to this statement and his version in court on a very material point.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of Amarchand who died in the previous year. The Income tax Officer assessed the total income of the deceased Amarchand to income tax under section 24B(1) read with section 24A of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that on a correct interpretation of section 24 B the amounts which were received by the heirs or legal representatives after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by Amarchand and liable to tax under s.24B(2). On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the income was taxable as the estate was liable for tax on the amounts received by her husband and that the Income Tax Officer was entitled to assess the total Income of the said deceased Amar Chand. The High Court in reference held that section 24BB did not apply to the case of the respondents and that section 23B was applicable only to cases where the income had already been received before his death but not after his lifetime. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 1, 2 and 3 of s. 24B. [707 G] (ii) The legal representatives have by fiction become liable for payment of income tax out of their estate. They are not liable to be taxed as income received after his demise but they are liable to pay out of the estate of the person who cannot be deemed to be assessees for the purpose of assessment in the several years of assessment. [807 C] (iii) The Explanation to section 24(1)(b) does not apply where a person dies before the publication of the notice referred to in sub s.(1) of section 22 or before he is served with a notice under sub section(2) of that section. It cannot be extended beyond the object for which it was enacted. [777 D] (iv) The words "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" indicate that they were income which may be deemed as taxable by fiction incorporated into sub s. (1). In the present case the amounts claimed to be taxable were those which were not received in the earlier year and were therefore not liable for taxation in the subsequent years.

The petitioners who were members of the Andhra Pradesh State Public Employment (Requirement to Residence) Rules, 1959 challenged the validity of the impugned orders on the ground that they contravened article 16(3) and Article 16(1) of the Constitution. The High Court quashed the orders holding that the power was given to Parliament under article 35(a) of tile Constitution and that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under article 32 of the constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the power to make a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State is not conferred by Parliament, and (ii) the Rules are ultra vires the Constitution and were therefore void. HELD: The contention that the impugned order is invalid cannot be accepted. It was not necessary for the Legislature to specifically provide for residence in any particular part of the State or any particular Part of it. [122 G] (i)(a) The power to legislate is given to the Parliament but is denied to the Legislatures of the States, notwithstanding anything in the Constitution, and under that Article the Parliament has been supreme and can make any law on the subject as the article stood, speaks of a whole State as the venue for residential qualification and it is impossible to think that the Constituent Assembly was thinking of residence in Districts, Taluqas, cities etc. more appropriate and specific language could have been used as such or any requirement as aforesaid could have be used as some 'any requirement as mentioned in article 35 (a) and (b). [122 C D] (ii)(a)(i) The expression "any requirement" is not defined in the Act but it has been defined in section 3 of the Act. It means a condition of employment in the State, or Union territory prior to such appointment or employment. [123 G H] (b) The word 'any ' in article 16 (3) refers to residence within that State and includes any requirement which is necessary for residence within the State. The expression 'any other requirement as contemplated by article 35 has been used in the context of residence within a State or Union Territory prior to appointment or appointment to an office under the Government of, or any local authority within its territory. [124 A B] (c) The words "any requirements" in article 15(3), are wide enough to include residence within one State and not necessarily within that other State. [125 C D E] (d) The object of the Article is to provide for a special case for the establishment of residence outside the State and for employment or appointment in any office under another State. It is not necessary that there should be a separate provision for residence of persons belonging to different States. [126 A B, 127 C D]. (e) The first clause emphasises that the requirement may be also as to residential qualification but it is difficult to think whether Parliament 's intention in this behalf was to make any such law on a subject as a condition or employment in that State or part of that State. If it chose to speak of residence, in parts of State, as it stood, there would be no question of delegation to the Central and/or State Governments to provide by rules for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code, but he was acquitted by the Additional Sessions judge, Bulandshahr. The High Court on appeal held that the prosecution had failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant and that the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to him which were found in an almirah of the house in which the appellant lives jointly with his father and that therefore he was not guilty of any of those acts. The appellant contended that the High Court had erred in holding that though the prosecution has merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house, some other articles belonging thereto were found therein and that they were in exclusive possession thereof. Held, that the mere fact that the account was not in the joint possession of himself and his father did not make it a case of theft but only in their joint possession. The fact that an officer of the post office had in the course of his duties access to postal articles by an officer or the post offices even though they may not have been entrusted to him or even though he might not have so secreted them from the mere facts that they are found in the almirah which is said to have been in their exclusive possession, did not affect the question as to whether the appellant had availed himself of the opportunity to procure articles. The mere fact of seizure and that being a question to be decided only by the Court of fact, this Court would not re examine the evidence for satisfying itself as to the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions reached by the High court.

The appellant, a Panchayat, was convicted under section 409 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to simple imprisonment for one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the Sarpanch had not been produced before the Panchayat; (ii) the Magistrate had not taken into consideration the affidavit and the telegram of Mahabir Chari, which was not accepted by the Nyaya Panchayat; and (iii) the High Court erred in holding that the five appellants had disobeyed an order staying proceedings pending before it staying proceedings before it stays. HELD : The High court did not appreciate that the Sarpanch who bad initially declared that the affidavit was not proper because it did not contain any date of the High Courts ' stay order; even a copy of the telegram was not attached to the application and the application seems to have been made after the proceedings on that date had commenced and evidence taken. [117 B C] (ii)(a) The High Courts were in error in holding: (1) that the procedure followed by the Panchayat before passing an order of stay was not correct; (2) that it did neither comply with its orders nor did it comply with their orders; (3) that there was no material on the record to show that the Panchas had accepted the objections raised by the Sarpanch andrencyed him about the impropriety of the petitioner 's affidavit; (4) that in certain cases proceedings could be adjourned to December 25, 1963, and (5) that even a certified copy of an telegram was attached to it.

The appellant was taken in custody and as a result of the investigation, he caused the death of Sheo Sahai. The prosecution case against him was that on June 13, 1960, one Paley Singh informed about the murder of Sheo Swarup. The appellant denied the allegation that he had caused the murder to Sheo Sahai and stated that he did not have any improbability in Ujagar Singh 's statement about the occurrence. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 302 I.P.C., but acquitted him on appeal, and confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The extra judicial confession together with the circumstances relied upon by the High Court were not admissible or not in evidence as there was good independent evidence with respect to the four matters mentioned in the report and relied on by the trial court. It is no doubt true that a person who commits a murder in pursuance of an enmity arising out of minor disputes, would be so justified in his conduct as to openly admit it to the first person he met and went to the Police Station for reporting about it. But this does not mean that the appellant should have made a statement that he was taking his bath at night in the Canal Distributory. The fact that he has the sword which was stained with human blood immediately after the murder is also supported by PaleY Singh, Paleiy Singh finds ample support from the facts that the accused had a bath in the canal at that hour. [208 C D] (ii) The High Court erred in rejecting the statement of Ujagar Singh about the appellant 's conduct in purchasing a sword and delivering it stained with blood immediately before the murder. It was no doubt possible that the deceased might have committed the murder but that does not necessarily mean that he should have been taken to the police station for reporting the matter. [209 G] (iii) The fact of the extra judicial confessions together with their circumstances relied on in the reports and relied upon in the case of the appellant, that a man who commits an enmity with Sheo Sahai had committed the crime of murder is not admissible nor in evidence. It may be that a conviction can be based solely on circumstantial evidence but it must be shown that the person who committed the offence was guilty of the crime. [210 C] (iv) The statement of Paleary Singh about his having seen the appellant committing the murder cannot be relied upon as there is good independent corroboration from the fact that the witness had seen the accused committing the crime and deposited it stained therewith with human Blood immediately after it was committed.

The appellants filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the electoral roll and the calendar events issued for the purpose of the said election. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules calling upon persons whose names had not been included in the electoral rolls and who claimed to be included in i.e., the appellants, and that the declaration of results of all the 44 successful candidates was liable to be quashed. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court by special leave against the judgment of the High court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court had rightly dismissed the petition on the ground that there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the petition and the delay was not satisfactorily explained. [419B] 2.2 In the instant case, the appellants were entitled to the issue of the writ prayed for as of right and the delayed filing of the petition should have been ignored. The delay in preferring the petition could be ignored. [520C D] 3.3 The High Courts had rightly rejected the writ application on the basis that it was only on December S, 1978 that the appellants knew that there had been an error in the notification issued under rule 4(i) of Rules notifying claims and objections to the inclusion of names in the said electoral roll. [620D] 3.(a) The High courts have rightly rejected a writ petition on this ground. [525E] (b) The appellants were not entitled to any relief as prayed for by them. [625G] 4(c) The delay was neither satisfactorily explained nor explained. There was no good explanation for such delay in the filing of an appeal.

The appellant company was a private limited company. It had its registered office at Hyderabad and it was carrying on business in the name of "M/s. Vulcan Industries (P) Ltd., a private company. The appellant company, as its directors, filed a complaint against the 1st respondent company and its directors for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that if no balance sheet was laid before a general body meeting before a special general meeting, there could be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220(1) of the 1956 Act or section 220 of the Companies Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (i) in a prosecution under section 134 of the 1913 Act, there can be no dispute that the balance sheets were not properly called and the balancesheet and profit account could not be laid before the general body; (ii) in any case, the requirement of sub section (2) of section 134 is mandatory and it does not make him liable u/s 220(I) of 1956 Act as the case may be, while wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balance Sheet and profit loss account before an annual general meeting was held; (iii) in the present case, there was no charge framed against the appellant because the general meeting had not been called and it could not rely upon its failure to call the general Body meeting as a defence to the prosecution. [407 D] The High court was right in taking the view that even if no charge sheet is laid before one general body, there cannot be any question of a balance sheet being not adopted nor complying with requirements of Section 220(2) Of 1956 Act.

The appellant was appointed as a Professor of Radiology in the respondent Institute. He was promoted to the post of Associate Professor of the concerned speciality on October 9, 1964 and was confirmed in that post on November 10, 1964. The appellant was promoted as Assistant Professor of radiography in the Maulana Azad Medical College on October 8, 1964, but he was not considered for appointment to the said post. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of his promotion as Associate Professor and the High court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant possessed the qualification and experience prescribed for appointment as Assistant Professors of Radiologist (ex officio) in the Irwin Hospital which is attached to the Ma Lady Azad Medical college, New Delhi. The High Court held that the designation of the appellant as a Radiologist was an academic post and that he had the essential educational qualifications and had also the requisite teaching experience while holding the post as Assistant professor of Radiography (exofficio) in Maulana Nehru Medical College. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The Ministry of Health cannot be heard to say that the Appellant has not acquired the status of an Associate Professor or Associate Professor in the Willingdon Hospital or the Safdarjang Hospital. [802C] 2.1 The Ministry is a public authority and it can be said that the teaching experience gained by the appellant was similar to that of honorary Professor or Assistant Professor in those speciality. It cannot be said, therefore, that the post held by the Appellant does not give him a right to hold the post. [820E] 2(a) The Ministry has been utilizing his services as such for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students of the MaAVE Azad Medical University which is a teaching hospital attached to it. That being so, it cannot be that the appel lant who was a Radiographer cum Associate Professor could not be considered for employment to the Post of Assistant Professor or Reader in the Hospital or Safdarjung Hospital. The question whether the appellant possesses the qualification or experience prescribed in Annexure I to the Second Schedule must be interpreted in a broad and liberal sense as it would otherwise work otherwise great injustice to persons in Specialists Grade II for a non teaching job. [821H; 802A] 2.(b) The Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966, which came into force on October 10, 1965, were not applicable to the appellant who was appointed to the supertime grade I for teaching post. It is also not possible to support the impugned action of the Government of India in holding that teaching experience obtained by the appeli lant as an Associate professor or Radiologist in the hospital could not give her a right of hold the said posts as Assistant professors of Radiological and/or Radiology (exminence) which the appellant holds in the Alwin Hospital. It was urged on behalf of the Union of India that the said teaching experience was an essential qualification for appointment of Associate Professors of radiologist cum Associate Professors and that the same was not a condition precedent to the appointment of the post, as required under the Central Health Services (Amendment). Rules, 1965. [822E F] 3.(c) The appellant having been substantively appointed to a non clinical post in the super time grade I, cannot be considered to have acquired the said status of a Professor or an Associate Reader of Radiologists. [823G H; 803A] 4(d) The Government of Delhi has been utilised by the University of Delhi for teaching and/and research purposes in that Institute. It may be true that the Ministry of Home Affairs is a welfare State, but it cannot take into consideration the fact that the Central Government has been utilized by the Universities of Delhi to teach and/ or research purposes.

The workmen of the appellant company were employed by the respondent company as casual workers in the appellant 's factory. The workmen claimed that they should be paid wages at the minimum rates of Rs.95 per month and that the Tribunal was wrong in fixing the minimum wages in accordance with the minimum wage prevailing in the Company on the basis of the minimum Wages prevalent in other industries in that region. The Tribunal held that there were no comparable industry in the same line of business as the Company in the region which could be compared with the Company, and that, therefore, the Tribunal should have proceeded to fix the minimum rate of wages in the company on the ground that there was no similar industry in that area. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and not at the time of reference. [723 B] (ii) The principle laid down by this Court in French Motor Co.(1) is not rigid and does not require that the minimum Wage prevailing in other concerns should be fixed at the average level of 'wages in the industry on the date of the award. In such cases, the calculation is still on the foundation of basic wage and dearness allowance. [823 C] (iii) The minimum wages so far as it consists of basic wages and dearness allowances are separately payable, the bonus is only calculated on the method of the Minimum wage prevailing at the point of time of award. [820 D E] (iv) The formula adopted by this court in French Car Co.(2) was not sound and did not require any interference.

The assessee was carrying on business under the Railways as well as the Government. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961 to the assessee for the assessment year 19. The assessee filed his return of income and claimed that he had made an incorrect statement in the return. The assessing officer rejected the assessee 's claim on the ground that it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the assessee to file a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal, the High Court held that the Commissioner was satisfied that it was a fit case for the issue of notice under Section 148 and that he could not have issued a fresh notice under s 148. It also held that since the assessee had made a wrong statement in his return, the Income tax officer had no jurisdiction to issue a notice unders. 148. In the appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The order sheet recording reasons of the Income Tax Officer does not set out any reason for coming to the conclusion on the material before him that he was satisfied about the existence of the belief that the income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for that year. [845 C] (2) In his report the Incometax Officer did not set forth any reason as to why he had not recorded himself in the report. The order sheets recording the reasons of income tax officer were not mentioned in the reports. [873 E] (3) The material that he did not record himself in a report was not mentioned therein on the basis of which it could be said that he has made an erroneous statement. It is clear from the report that he merely stated "yes" and affixed his signatures thereunder. He did not say anything about the omission or failure on the part of these assessee to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for the accounting year in question.

The appellant, who was at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939 carrying on any business, profession or vocation on which tax was at any time charged under the provisions of the Act of 1918, was succeeded in such capacity by another person, the change not merely being a change in the constitution of a partnership, no tax shall be payable by the first person mentioned in respect of the income, profits and gains of the said period. The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant for the assessment year 1939 40 under the Indian Incometax Act, 1918, but on appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that as a result of this splitting up there was a discontinuance of the original business at the date of the partition and on such discontinuance, the family became entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the Income tax Act. The appellant 's appeals were dismissed by the Appellate Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the business must have been charged to tax under the Act Of 1918 and he was not liable to pay tax for the period between April 13, 1938 and March 28, 1939; (ii) the original firm ceased to exist and its business was carried on thereafter by two independent firms, for the document of October 30, 1943 had referred to annexures C 1 and C 11 as constituting two independent partnerships and proceeded to revoke them and (iii) the family ceased to be entitled to reliefs under section25(3). HELD: The question whether the appellate firm was entitled to the benefits of section 25 (4) of Income tax. Act, 1922, is one which has been quoted in the judgment of this Court in Commissioner of Income Tax vs M/s. K. C. Dastoor & Co., [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 869. The question is whether the Appellate firm was liable to be assessed under the Income Tax Act, on the ground that it had taken place in 1948 and its Business was carried out thereafter by one independent firms for the documents of October 31, 1943.

The appellant, a Hindu widow, filed a suit for partition of the properties in the Court of the Sub Judge, Khandappa. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit properties belonged to the joint family and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7/24th share. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the property belonged to his joint family, that the decree of the trial court was not fully justified and that on a true view of law, the widow 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband's life time. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the widow had no prior or partition; (ii) the suit property belonged only to the family, and (iii) the wife will take equally, each having one share in the coparcenary property on the hypothesis of a partition between himself and his sons. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The interest of a Hindu Mist coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in that property if a partition of that property had taken place immediately before his death. [724B] 2. In order to ascertain the share of the deceased in the property that would have been allotted to him if a division of the property had took place immediately prior to his death, there must be some evidence to show that the share was actually allotted to the appellant or she received or must be deemed not to have received in the notional partition. [765C] 3. The fictional, however, expedient to ascertain share of heirs in the ancestral property has to be determined according to the terms of the testamentary instrument if any, made by the deceased. In an important aspect, the case is stronger in the matter of working out the fictional that the interest of the Hindu Mist Mitakshara coparcener shall he deemed to have been given in the joint property because after all, the plaintiff 's husband and his children had a 1/4th share therein. [76B C] 4. The mere fact that there is no prior family partition or that there has been a partition during the life time between the plaintiff and his brothers does not make any difference. [77C D] 5. In the instant case, by application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Act, whatever be the shares of the coparcenary properties would devolve upon the surviving members of the family. The only step is to ascertain whether the share had actually taken place before his lifetime. [75E] 6. In a case where the plaintiff has a 1st share in a coparcenary property, the partition of which takes place immediately after his death is effected between him and his two sons, there would be four sharers in the family property on one side of a joint Hindu Family property. The first step also to ascertain what the share has actually taken from the deceased has to find out the share that the deceased had in the coparcener 's property. [78F G] 7. In view of this position, whatever was the share at the time of his death in the Mitakshara coparcenary property would devolve on the surviving member of the joint Hindu family. [79C D; 77A] 8. The High Court rightly held that there had been a severance of the interest and the plaintiff had no right to claim partition. The fact that the widow was not given any share in her ancestral property does not alter the position of the appellant 's father. [80F G].

The appellant Corporation was established in the year 1962. The age of retirement of its employees was 58 years and at that time there were no rules framed under the Act for the purpose of fixing the age of superannuation. The appellant Corporation, however, made a representation to the State Government on September 3, 1966, requesting that it should retire on completion of 58 years of age and at any time thereafter on giving three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. The State Government rejected the said representation by its order dated October 17, 1968. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the employees of the Corpo ration who were employed after the Corporation was estab lished, that is, after 1st September 1956 they were entitled to continue in service till 60 years of their age and as a Class III employee belonging to Class I or Class II appointed to the service of the Corporation on or after 1 st September, 1956 had to retire on completing 58 years. The writ petition filed by the appellant Corporation challenging the legality of the order was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the employees belonging to class I and Class II were not entitled to continued in service beyond the age Of 60 years as a class III employee; (ii) the provisions of regulation 19(2) of the Regulations which affected the employees who became the employees on 1st October, 1956 could not be said to have been applicable to the transferred employees who had entered service of Corporation after 1.9.1956 and were entitled only to continue beyond the date of age of 58; (iii) the amendment of regulation 20 empowered the appointing authority to extend at its discretion the service conditions of any employee of the corporation on or before 1st November, 1956, to retire from service on completion Of 58 years; and (iv) the amended regulations were not applicable to employees who joined the service after 1th September, 1957. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court erred in striking down regulation 19 (2) as amended in 1977. [223B] 2.1 It is well settled that the power of the appointing authori ty to extend the age at any point of time thereafter cannot be said either to have vested in the employee or to his successor in office. In other words, the power to extend has been conferred on the appointing authorities by the relevant regulations. The Regulations are not intended to confer a new right on the employee who had joined service after the date when he was appointed to a Class I post. [224C] 2(a) The employees of a private sector establishment, the Central Government and the State Governments services and the Central Govern ment services cannot be equated with those who joined service before 1 st November,1956. [225D] (b) The Central Government or the State Govern ment Services are not covered by any of the regulations. They are governed by the provisions contained in the Act. [226E] 2.(a) In the instant case, the employees were appointed to Class III posts after 1nd September, 1955 and they had entered into service of a Corporation on being appointed to that class I post after 1St September,1956 and they were not governed by any regulations. [227D] 3(b) It is only in 1965 under the settlement and the amendment in the Regulations that the age o f superannuation of employees of Class III and Class IV was 58. The Central Governmen ts and the Government services and State Government services were governed by a new sub regulation which was notified on September, 1, 1956. [228E] 4(c) The High Courts erred in strike down Regulation 19(1)(2) which affected employees who have joined service of respondent No.

The appellants, who were members of the Bar Association of Charkhi Dadri, filed a complaint against the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court alleging that the Chief Minister of Haryana and the Prime Minister had committed contempt. The Chief Justice was also impleaded as party respondent No. 2 in the criminal case. The appellants contended before the Full Bench that the letter written by them to the President of India could not be construed as scandalising the Hon 'ble Judge or the Chief Judge in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice. The High Court did not take any action against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech. The Full Bench referred to paragraph 9 of the affidavit where the deponents stated that the contents of the letter were supported by the deponent himself and that the appellants had no intention whatsoever on their part to scandalize the Honble Judges or to weakens in any way the confidence of the people in the Administration of justice, and that there was no intention whatever on his part to contempt. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The letter does not constitute contempt. It is no part of the duty of a Judge nor it is a duty of the Judge or of the Hon ble Court in discharge of office of office. [246F] 2. The contents thereof a prima facie case constituted contempt. There was nothing to show that the matter did not constitute any contempt. In fact, the letter referred to the letter of the appellant and said "on a perusal of the contents thereof, a primafacie case is made out." [246G H] 3. The deponent tenders his apology to this Hon ' ble Court for the same and prays for its acceptance. [248F] 4. The contemnor tendered his apology in court. The affidavit referred to in the notice refers to paragraph 10 of the Affidavit where the deponent tenders unconditional apology. It was not a contempt. [249G H; 249A] 5. The statement made by the deponent that the letters were supported with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon'ble Judge of his personal views on political matters would be more sorry than the deponent herself. The deponents said that the allegations in the letter constitute contempt of court. [250F] 6. The allegation in the affidavit is that the deponent tendered apology to the Court and prayed for its rejection. The respondent No 2, a member of the bar Association of the Charkhikot, Bhiwani, has been placed for the consideration of this Bench. The full Bench referred the letter to the Chief Secretary of Haryana.

The petitioner, Suraj Mall Mohta & Co. (Porus) Ltd., was prosecuted under section 5(1)(d) of the Income tax Act for having evaded payment of income tax on income, and in respect of certain other points as mentioned in sub section (4) of section 5 of the impugned Act, he claimed that the provisions of the Act were void. The High Court held that the said sections contravened article 14 of the Constitution and quashed the proceedings. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioner that the impugned sections violated articles 14 and 19(1) (d) and (6) of article 14 and that the procedure prescribed by the Act was a good substitute for that prescribed by section 5, i.e., section 7, and that as such an enquiry into the validity of sub section 4 of the said Act was not referred to the Commission under the provisions Of the impugned Acts, it was not open to the Central Government to add to the number of persons included in section 5 (1) of that Act, and as such the procedure adopted by the Commission was a valid substitute for those prescribed by sections 5(4), 6(5) and 6(8). HELD: The provisions of sub sections (4), (7) and 5 of section 4 are not confined to any period and this certainly operates to the detriment of those dealt with under sub section(4) Of section 5. [454 E] In the present case, the two procedures were different in so far as they affect the persons proceeded against under that sub section being a piece of discriminatory legislation violative of article 13 of the constitution and is thus void and unenforceable. The impugned sections are therefore not hit by article 14.

The respondent, a trade union of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi (Appellant 2) is a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops ,and Establishments Act, 1954. The Federation of Indian Chamber of Commerce & Industry, Delhi (Respondent 1) is an "industrial establishment" under the Act. The respondent, an association of all its members, carried on in the premises in question, a "business", within the definition of "commercial establishments". The Federation filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the activities of the Federation carried on by it amounted to "work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary to trade" within section 2 (5) Of the Act, and that the activity of the respondent was a "trade", within its meaning. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The definition of 'commercial establishment ' given in the Act is wide enough to include activities carried on for profit. It does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. [352C] The very definition refers to "any work in connection or incidental to trade". It does nothing more than what a profit, but it will bear repetition that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and that it does not merely amount to "business" within its ambit of section2(5). [352D] The definition is wide and comprehensive enough to cover activities carried out by the Federation as a whole. It includes activities which are incidental or incidental. It cannot be said that the functions of a "shop" or a " commercial establishment" are not "business". [352E F] In the instant case, the activity carried on was a business or trade. The definition does not indicate that the services of a registered society, charitable or other association of any individual traders, industrialists or businessmen. It is also not distributed among its members. The fact of the matter is that the respondent is a Federation of all their members.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of one Sri Babu Ausan Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. The income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the receipt of the appellant as an allowance during the previous year of assessment was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. The High Court in reference under the Act answered the question in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The source of the pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land within the definition of agricultural Income as defined in section 2(1)(a) of that Act. [737 B] (ii) The sources of the income still remain the arrangement and not land. It is true that the source of pension is a liability incurred by the government for extinguishing proprietary rights, but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. But in this case no material has been produced to show that the allowance varied from year to year, the source and character of the property still remains the arrangement. [837 C] (iii) The income was a revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. The source and nature of the right in which a fraction of the net income of an assessee is to be appropriated by the appellantas his remuneration is not in the right to receive rent or revenue of agricultural lands, but lies in the condition that it is the Government 's statutory obligation to pay it, and this obligation is not land under the definition in section 4 (3)(ix) of Act.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Chargemen 'A ' in various ordnance factories between 1962 to 1966. They were promoted as Chargeman II on completion of two years ' service and their promotion thereafter could be effected only in accordance with the normal Rules and not merely on the completion of 2 years ' satisfactory service but also on completion o f two years' satisfactory service. The petitioners, who had been recruited in 1963 and those who had joined service in 1964, were promoted to the post of Chargeman I on completion af two years of continuous service on the basis of the Rules. They filed writ petitions before this Court praying for a direction to the respondents to give them the benefit of promotion only on completion fic ers of two year ' service as Charge Man in various orders of 1966 and 1968. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief for the period for which they had completed their 2 years service on completion Of two years service. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The service rule contemplated that there has to be no work i.e. a person will not be entitled to a py and allowance during the period of his continuous satisfactory service even though he was given a proper place in the gradation list havi ng been promoted as chargeman II. [109F] 1.2. The seniority list prepared by the Madhya Pradesh Hi gh Court on 4th April, 1983 is not challenged. It is now well settled that there can be no question of automatic promotion merely because some Supervisors have been appointed as chargemen ' A ' and were granted promotion as Charge man II. The respondents in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 are entitled to be treated as Charge I for the purpose of promotion from the date their junior was promoted. [110G H] 1.(a) In so far as Supervisors 'A who claimed promotion as charge Man ation II, the High Court had rightly disallowed the relief for his claim for the benefit that he had been appointed in 1963 or thereafter. [111F G] (b) The High Courts have rightly held that there was no scope for automatic promotion only because some Supervisor having been en promoted asChargeman II, had not been promoted to higher post with effect from 1st April, 1982. [11G H; 11A] 2.1 In so much as Supervisors who claimed the promotion ascharge I or in about the year 19 66 they chose to wait for about 17 years to file these writ petitions which were filed after the decision dated 2nd February, 1981 was delivered by this Court either the subsequent order dated 28th December, 1965 or circular dated 20th January, 1966 and the legal consequences flowing therefrom. [112F G H] 2.(a). The High Cou rt has rightly held in its judgment that there had to be a proper promotion only when some Supervisors having been appointed on the date of completion of their 2 yea rs service as Supervisor 'A were not promoted aschargeman II and some of them have even been enfaced satisfactory service, and therefore, they could not be promoted inasmu tially. [114G H, 115B] (c) The appellants in Civil Appeals No. 442 of 1981 and the petitioners in Civil appeal No. 771 of 1981 were entitled to get the same relief as was granted by this court to such of the appellants in the said Civ il Appeal No 441 of1981.

The State Transport Undertaking, which was a private operator of the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, had granted permits to the private operators for operating in any inter State route. The State Transport Undertakings were granted permits under section 68 F(1) of the Act for the transport of tourism on the routes specified therein. The permit holders applied for stage carriage permit from the State Transport undertaking to operate in the inter State routes. The Regional Transport Authority, Bangalore, rejected their applications and directed that they should be given preference to private operators who had not got a certificate of approval from the Central Government. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the proviso to section 63(7) of Chapter IV A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the proviso was not violative of article 14 of the Constitution and that the fourth sub clause of the Proviso to section 68F(1 H) did not offend article 14. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the State transport Undertaking would have preference in the matter of stage carriage permits; (ii) the exclusion contemplated by section 68G(7), which is unconstitutional and violative of Article 14, was not attracted because the proviso did not violate article 14; and (iii) the fourth clause of proviso to Section 63(1H) applied with equal force to the preference provided for in section 47(1). Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The general scheme of the , in the matters of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the case of a notified route or notified route, such permit shall be granted to the State Government by the State Road Transport Undertaking by the Central Govt., in respect of such number of tourist vehicles as the Central Gov. may, in respect thereof, specify in this behalf, and the provisions of sections 49, 51, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64 shall, as far as may be applicable, apply in relation to such permits. [1015B C] 2. The proviso to sub section (7) does not say that the permit shall he granted to private operator for operating any inter state route without detriment to its responsibility for providing efficient and adequate road transport services in any notified area or notified routes. It is clear from the language of the second proviso that the State Govt. has the discretion to grant preference to all applicants on merits, applying the rules of preference provided by the proviso. [1005D] 3. The third sub clause does not contemplate a situation where the State Governments have the power to grant permits to private parties for operating inter state routes in any Inter State route without prejudice to their responsibility for ensuring efficient and effective road transport service in any other region.
