[666 C D] (4) Rule 23A is beyond the rule made by State Government, either under Section 19(I) or section 20(2) of Act. It follows therefore that Rule 23 A is intra vires of rule making powers of State government either under s.19(i), or s.

The appellant was a Government servant. He was dismissed from service by the Inspector General of Prisons, Saurashtra, on the ground that he had failed to supply a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer and that the order of dismissal was illegal and void on the grounds that it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. The High Court held that there was no duty to supply the copy of report of an enquiry officer amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311 (2). In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The order of discharge was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability in respect of an actionable wrong as it contravened articles 311(1)(a), (b) and (c) of article 311. [922 C] (2) The High court erred in fastening the liability in regard to arrears of pay on the State of Maharashtra. [ 923 D] (3) The appellant was not concerned with the second contention but it was a dispute between the State Government and the State. It is true that some elements of relationship between a public servant and Government are based on contract within the meaning of section 60(2)(a) of that Act. But, however, that some element of relationship exists between a private servant and an Government servant for the period that he was actually in office. [977 E] (4) The words "actionable wrong" in this context are wide words and include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government employee for arrears of salary earned by a public man for the time during which he has served. [980 F G] (5) The word 'proved ' in this clause means something more or less than tortanty and not an error to determine.

The appellant, a lessee of the respondent 's land, entered into an agreement with the respondents for the purpose of carrying on mining operations in the area. The appellant was to construct a road over the said land and remove the coal from the said area. On the basis of the aforesaid agreement the appellant made an application under section 80 of the Indian Mines Act, 1923, for permission to cut down the boundary line between the two leaseholds. The respondents resisted the claim on the ground that the appellant had encroached upon the respondent land and removed the coal therefrom. The Subordinate Judge held that the respondents were in possession of the land as tenants and that they could not be evicted from the land. On appeal, the Subordinate Judge reversed the decision of the Subordinate judge and decreed the suit. In second appeal to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the boundary between the parties was clearly demarcates the boundary lines between the appellants ' holding and the respondents ' holding that article 48 of the Limitation Act applied to the suit and that the appellants were entitled to the reliefs prayed for. Held, that the concurrent finding of fact arrived at by the courts below in respect of this issue was not correct. The High Court had rightly held that under the Indian mines Act and the Rules made thereunder the plaintiffs were bound to keep a barrier of 25 feet to the south of the defendant 's working and, therefore, the boundary could more satisfactorily and definitely be fixed with reference to the plans annexed to the subsequent lease deeds executed in favour of the respondents. The appellants had failed to prove that they had knowledge of the sinking of the quarries and pits in the encroached area.

The appellant was a crosscutter. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The Secretary and others threatened the appellant with physical violence. The appellant terminated his services under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry and the order was communicated to him. In appeal, the Industrial Tribunal held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman and thereafter departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r., 18(b). The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the action taken under rr. 18 (a) and 18(c) of Standing Orders. The High Court held that this was a colourable exercise of power conferred by r.18(a), and therefore its action could not be upheld as a bona fide exercise of the power under r, 18(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the employer wanted to take departmental action against him under r 18(A) and (ii) the order terminating his services was mala fide and was therefore invalid. HELD: (i)(a) The question whether the employer could defend the action under r.(18(b) of r. 19(a). [619 F] (b) The power conferred on the employer by r 18 (A) is a colourable legislative exercise of its power and it cannot be said that the industrial court has the right to inquire into causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18( A) and if the terminaton of service is a device of victimisation or unfair labour practice it would be prejudiced if Sankaran were retained in service. [620 C] (ii)(a). The employer could not defend the actions taken under R. 18.(b) because, in the present case, the appellant failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise of his power in this case was mala fides and was not colourable exercise Of the power conferred under r 19(c).

The appellant, a cinematograph theatre, was granted a lease of the said premises in favour of the respondent No. 1 for a period of five years from November 27, 1954 to March 31, 1955. The agreement provided that the lessee would be entitled to terminate the tenancy and to continue the same till the expiry of the term of the lease. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 claiming a declaration that it was entitled under the agreement dated December 1, 1960, and further confirmed by document dated November 27 1954, as confirmed by the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960. The Trial Court decreed the suit on the ground that the consent order had not decided that the transaction between the parties of the year 1954 was in the nature of a lease or other character having to be decided at the trial and the consent judgment in suit NO. 149 was barred by the principle of res judicata. In appeal, the High Court held that the agreement was not a lease but only an oral one and that it had no effect on the rights of the parties. The High Court also held that as the agreement of November 27. 1954 created a lease, the consent decrees were not binding on the appellant. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The agreement dated November 28, 1954 was a lease and that the Consent decree in favour was not enforceable by law. [401 B] (2) The question whether the legal relationship arising out of the agreement between the appellant and his landlord and falling within the purview of section 28 of the Bombay Rent Control Act is derived from section 28 or whether it was a case decided within the meaning of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, was not raised before the High court. [442 C] (3) The consent decree created by the agreement did not decide that question and therefore the consent was not binding. It was not open to the appellant to raise this question again in revision at this stage. [441 D E] (4) The decision of the Trial Court as confirmed in appeal was a judgment by consent, decree or order in the suit No 149 of 1961.

The respondent was appointed as a Pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force on 1.6.1972 and was confirmed in that post on 30.8.1985. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer on 2.9.1986. The respondent challenged his reversion before the High Court contending that he was entitled to salary upto the period he was not entitled to remain in service, as he had been granted a permanent commission in the Air Force and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F.S. The High Court allowed the Review Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ Petition was liable to be dismissed. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the High court had erred while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24.3.1988, which had been passed in the Writ petition on 10.7.1986, that the order could be sustained only if there was a further extension and not beyond that date unless there was an order of extension. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court while settingaside the order dated 26.7 1988 had rightly set aside the same by its judgment dated 24th March,1988 passed in Writ Petition on merits as it did on 24.03.1988 which had not been extended by the Governor beyond 30th August, 1985. [243E F] 1.2 The High Courts while setting up the Review Peti tion Petition claiming to be reinstated in service irrespective of the merits of the case and the extent of his right, have rightly set out the reasons for dismissing the Writ Appeal on merits. [244F G] 1.(a) In the instant case, the High Courts had not considered the claim of the respond ent as a matter of fact that his term of office had come to an end on 30th September, 1985 and no further order of extention had been issued by the Govern ment beyond 30st August,1985. [245G] 1(b) The High courts while setting out the interim order dated 10.07.1986 passed in writ petition on 24th April, 1988 had not taken into consideration the fact that the respondent was entitled t o be reinstated and no observations in this regard were made by the Court. [242A B] 2.(a)(i) In view of the fact as stated above, it is open for the opposite parties to consider the claim for reinstatement in service regardless of the merit of the claim and the area of his rights. The interim order did not and could not amount to a direction that the respond ant was entitled lo be reinstated into service irrespective the merits or the extent Of his right. [246F G; 246A] 3.(b) In any case, it would be open for opposite parties t o consider the claims of the petitioner for continution of service in a particular period after his first appointment and he should be treated as regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till 30th of August, 1984 when there was no order of re spondent extending his period of appointment till 30.08.1985 or even though there was such an extension.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The prosecution case was that the deceased Subhadramma was the wife of the appellant and she used to stay in the house of the deceased 's mother. She was married about one and a half years before the occurrence. The accused used to visit his wife and often used to keep her in the same house. The deceased was also assaulted by the accused with a knife which he was carrying on his wife. The appellant was acquitted by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the discrepancies found by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and that they have been unduly magnified by the learned Sessions Judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. [368E] 2. In the instant case, the prosecution tried to make out a strong suspicion against the appellant that he was stabbing his wife in the manner suggested by the prosecution and when two views were possible, the benefit of doubt should be given to the accused. The evidence which is corroborated by the medical evidence on record shows that the injuries must have been caused in the way suggested by P.W. 1 to 3 or the evidence of P. W. I to 3. [367F G] 3. In view of the evidence which was corroborated by what was mentioned in exhibit P. 1, the appellant could not be said to have been prejudiced by the possibility of a duality of views, the High court should not interference with the orders merely because other view is possible. The appeal must accordingly fail. [369G H] 4. In order to entitle an accused person to the benefit Of doubt arising from the possibility Of a dual line of views the prosecution must be beset with fanciful doubts, rejects evidence for slender reasons and takes a view of that evidence in favour of the accused must be reasonable. [370B C] 5. The fact that some of the villagers who had gathered there were two divergent versions given by the Prosecution and the defence and when one views were available, the accused is entitled to the benefits of doubt. [371F G H] 6. In a case where an order of conviction is reversed, the appellate court should interfere with it only because another reasonable view is equally possible. If the evidence is so strong against the accused, the Court should interfere in the interest of justice lest the administration of justice be brought to ridicule.

The appellant, a public servant, was convicted by the Special Judge under Section 5(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having committed an offence punishable under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of that Act. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had not been given a reasonable opportunity to defend himself and that the provisions of Section 6(1) (c) were not applicable to the case of a Judge of the Supreme Court or the High Court, as the case may be. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the expression "inappliable to a Judge" in clause (e) must be construed in its widest sense and should be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authority under Section 6. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word "in Appliable" in section 6(i)(c) is not used in the sense of "any other person". It is used in a wider sense and includes persons who are not members of that House or of the Legislature. [419B C] 2. Section 6 (1) of Prevention of corruption Act,1947 is applicable to cases where the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. The words "in any other case" in sub section (2) of section 6 are strong enough to make it obligatory for the President or the Chief Justice of India, as he may think fit, to appoint and to remove a Judge from his office by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of not less then two thirds of not more then two members of the House and by a minority of not exceeding two third of not then two fourths of the members of such House. [520C D] 3. The framers of the Constitution, while dealing with such constitutional functionaries do not fall within the purview of the Act. They only contemplated their removal from office in accordance with clause (4) of Article 124 read with Article 2, Article 124 and (5) of article 124 read together with Article 124(4). [521D E] 4. The provisions of section 5 of Prevention Of Corruption Act 1947 are strong reasons to hold that Section 6 is inappliable for a Judge under the provisions contained in clauses (a) and (b) of sub section 2 of section 7 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. [525E F] 5. The language used in clause(e) is clear pointer in the direction that the Parliament has not yet considered it expedient to enact any law for the trial and punishment for that offence and for that purpose such constitutional functionary do not fell within the ambit of the expression 'inappaura ' occurring in clause 4 and 5 of Article 125 read with article 124(5). [525G H] 6. The Legislature did not enact any other law even for the investigation into allegations of corruption against a superior Judge and for his trial and sentence for that offences provided in clauses 4 and5 of Article 126 read with Art 124(1), even for investigation into charges of corruption by a superior judge, except by the previous sanction under clause (c). [421D] 7. The expression "any person" occurring in sub clause (a)(e), in the context of clause (f) is a clear pointer to that the Legislature did no such vertical hierarchy and the Chief Judge of India having no power of superintendence even over the High Courts, since the Chief justice of India is not a vertical hierarchy. [504E F; 516A] 8.

The appellant was a member of the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 of the Schedule Caste. He challenged the election on the ground that he belonged to a smaller group of Sunri caste which had nothing to do with Sunri and that it was, therefore, not open to him at the trial to contend that the Sahas were originally a smaller caste group within the Sunri community. The Tribunal held that item 40 included Sahas in Schedule Caste specified therein but did not claim, by virtue of abundant caution, so that the appellant bore the surname Saha holding that item40 excluded Sahas from Sunri. The High Court set aside the order of the Tribunal and directed the election of the appellant to be set aside on the grounds that the respondent belonged to an independent caste which was a smaller one. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent (i) that the word 'Saha ' in item 41 meant "a person belonging to a larger group" and not a member thereof, and (ii) that there was no evidence before the Tribunal that the said Sahas formed a sub caste within the meaning of item 40. HELD: (1) The word ' Saha ' in the expression 'excluding Saha ' is a caste, the word "Saha" in the clause must be read as including Saha ' excluding Saha ' and not merely Saha '. [390 B] (2) In the present case the appellant had established that the sub caste of Sahas was a larger one. The fact that the appel lant belonged to the smaller group called Sahas did not show that there were within the said Sunri, by reason of abundant precaution so that Sahas who bore the traname Saha could claim, without more. [391 C D] (3) In view of the matter, the correct interpretation of item 41 was that Saha's name was a sub Caste and had not been proved to belong to the larger group called 'Saha" within the concept of Sunrri caste.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent No. 2, who was the second respondent in this appeal. The appellant had entered into negotiations with the complainant and paid him Rs. 29,500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat. The complainant agreed to pay these sums on 4 12 1948, and paid them the two sums of money. The first sum of Rs. 1,000 was paid by the appellant and recovered the balance due in respect of the furniture and the other documents that were handed over to him by the complainant. The second respondent, who had been in possession of a flat, filed a complaint against the appellant under section 19(2) of the Act for the recovery of the sum of money on the ground that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his absence and that the police would give him Rs . 29,000 as consideration. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 18(1) of Act. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the word "relinquishment" was not a term of art and was used in the Transfer of Property Act and sentenced him to imprisonment for a term which may extend to 6 months and shall also be punhed with fine which shall not be less than the sum or value of the consideration received by him. The High Court, on appeal, held that it was intended by the legislature that "relish ment" should have the limited meaning sought to be placed upon it on behalf of the appellant, the word 'relinquish ment ' in its comprehensive sense as giving up possession of premises; and he had also charged under section19(2), sub clause (i) of section 18 for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relinishment by a tenant or person acting on behalf thereof. Held, that the words "relivish ment", used in section 108, sub clause(i) Of the Trans ference of Property would have been more appropriate than the words 'requisitioned possession of any premises; but the relinquishment of a tenancy is equivalent to surrender by the lessee or tenant of his rights as such. The consent of the landlord to the transfer of a lease by sub lease or otherwise, and it provides that the landlord who receives any fine premium, premium or other like sum or deposit or any consideration for the grant, renewal or continuance of a licence would be guilty of an offence and liable to the punishment specified therein.

The appellant, a workman in the category of Draftsmen and Rs. 150/ in the case of Draughtsman and Rs 100/ in other categories, was awarded an increase of Rs.150/ in respect of Draftsman and other workmen in the said category of Draughtsmen. The Industrial Tribunal held that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The award dated December 20, 1978 was intended to apply only to each individual workman, who would also have to get additional pay of Rs 150/ and Rs 200/ in case of Draftsm and Rs 150 / in the other categories. [150F] 2. The increase in the basic pay of individual workmen was intended in the original wage and, therefore, fell into error of amending the award. It was clearly intended by the Tribunal as is evident from the reference to "flat increase of pay" and not "ad hoc increase of salary". [150G H] 3. The Tribunal had only revised the wage scales by increasing the salary on entry into the service and res 184 tructuring the scale of pay, and not granting any ad hoc increase in salary to all employees. It could not be said that the figure of Rs 100 or in the present case of draftsmen was intended only to apply each individual workmen, there was nothing in the body of the award to indicate that it was intended by it to apply all those workmen, who were to get an ad hoc increases of salary. [151F] 4. The additional and basic question considered by the Industrial Tribunal was betrayed by a curious confusion in accepting the plea of the union that a flat increase to the pay of each individual employee was intended, while the iron was still hot as it was still not as it were hot as they were, the iron being still hot. [152G H; 153A] 5. The fact that some round flat or ad hoc increased salary to every employee, who belonged to the Union staff, there is nothing in paragraph 23 of the Award to indicate any such increase. It would obviously result in serious anomalous situations. While raising industrial disputes for revision of wage scales are certainly minded about their future prospects in the matter of wages, they would surely be more concerned with the immediate benefits according to them. [153A B] 6. The question whether a flat or an ad interim increase of one per month was intended or not was essentially a question of fact and it could not have been decided by the industrial Tribunal as a matter of fact. It is well settled that the jurisdiction of the Industrial Court under section 10(1)(c) of the Act is limited to the question whether the dispute is within the jurisdiction or not. [154E F] 7. The expression "future prospects" in the definition of "daily wage" has been defined by the Act as including "the minimum wages payable to a workman". It is clear from the definition that the word "d Daily wage" means "a sum which is paid for the work done by an employee in respect or in connection with his employment. The term "dwelling out" is not defined in the Act. [155F G] 8. The word "wages" has not been defined in any of the provisions of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. It means "any sum paid for work done in accordance with the terms and conditions of a contract". The definition of 'daily wages ' is wide enough to include all allowances payable to an employee for performing his duties. [156F] 9. The words "wages payable" are not defined by any of these provisions. It has been used in the sense of "wages". The word 'wages ' is not capable of precise definition.

The appellant paid its employees only for the period of 1/2/ per day and not for any other period. The appellant paid their employees only on the basis that they were paid wages at the rate prescribed by the award. The respondents contended before the Labour Court that the refusal to pay them wages was illegal as it amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. Held, that the terms prescribed by an award in a industrial dispute between the employer and his employees were not binding on the parties and the appellant had no right to make any change in them. The fact that the rates of wages fixed by an Industrial Tribunal cannot be said to amount to a contract of employment, and since an award made by an industrial tribunal cannot be held to be a contract between the parties when they deal with disputes arising out of the contract of service, express or implied, were not well founded. The terms of the agreement of employment either express or implicit, are not necessarily in question. It is only when the terms of employment are clear and unambiguous that the same can be done by an employer without any ambiguity or doubt. The words "in accordance with the terms" in section 2(vi) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, mean "a sum which is capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would if the terms were not express and could be implied". The word "compensation" in the context of industrial adjudication means all remuneration capable of having been expressed in term of money. It does not include wages fixed under any award or settlement between the employers and workmen. The expression "compensation ' in section 1(vi), therefore, includes wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudication.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed criminal misconduct and was convicted both under section 465 and section 409 Of the Indian penal Code. The High Court acquitted him but on appeal by special leave it was contended that the conviction of the appellant was illegal as sanction had not been obtained under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and that there being an acquittal of the accused by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate Court. Held: (i) The prosecution which has resulted in the conviction was initiated without any sanction under section197(1), and the absence of such sanc tion is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. (ii)The prosecution which had resulted in his conviction was instituted without any prior sanction under s 197(I) of Code of Civil Procedure, but that having been done by him while he was actually engaged in the performance of official duties, it could not arise at the stage of sanction, and the appellant could be prosecuted under s 409. The question whether sanction was necessary under section 198(1)(a) of Criminal P.C., was not raised before the High Court. (iii)The fact that the prosecution which was launched without any sanctioned sanction under the Act had resulted into the conviction did not support the contention that the appellant had been prosecuted under sections 409 and 420 of the I.P.C. The absence of sanction under that section was fatal to its maintainability.

The appellant, a resident of the erstwhile State of Cochin, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, Travancore. The appellant claimed that it had incurred in the erstwhile state of Cochin for the assessment years 1947 48 and 1949 49, and that the business losses incurred in British India could not be set off against the profits made in the former State of Travancore. Held, that the mere use of the words " income or gains accruing or arising to him within British India" in section 10(2)(c) of the Indian Act did not justify the construction. The mere use by the words 'income or gains ' in any other head could not by virtue of the proviso to sub section (1) of section 24 be set aside except for profits and gains accruing in British Indian or in an Indian State, but that is done under section 8 of the Act. The fact that the word " income" was used did not support an interpretation in favour of the disintegration of the head ' business and compel the application of the first proviso to section 24(1) which correspond to section 23(1). The mere fact that a word "income or profits" is used does not justify such construction. Commissioner of Income tax vs H. C. D. Tulloch, , referred to. The expression "income" in the proviso must be construed as meaning income accruing or arise within British Indian and not outside India. The words "income accruing or arises" in that proviso must mean business in British England and not in India.

The respondent company was a Company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Company was governed by the provisions of the Indian , and its employees were governed by an agreement entered into between the Company and its employee at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the condition that the age should be fixed at 60. In the course of the proceedings before the Tribunal, the company raised a dispute as regards the age Of retirement at 60 years. The Tribunal held that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the age at 60 and not at 55. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Tribunal was wrong in fixing the age for retirement at 58 years. It was not correct to say that the practice which the Tribunal has failed to notice is wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. What the Tribunal had failed to note was that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns, the trend had been tending the trend that the recent trend in the Bombay region was incorrect. The trend in Gujarat region was correct and it was not possible to say whether the trend was in Bombay or not at all as to how long ago the age was fixed at 58. [434 C D] (ii) The award made by the Tribunal is, therefore, wholly insufficient. It is well settled that the Tribunal should have regard to the relevant factors and materials disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on this record. In most of the cases, the age must be fixed as 60. The fact that in some of the awards there was a general agreement that the retirement age of superannuation at 60 would be 60 or 58 is not sufficient to indicate that instances which may justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an earlier occasion and were confirmed by this Court in some subsequent years are, in our opinion, wholly inadequate to indicate no slowingdown of this practice. [534 D E] (iii) The fact of the matter that the award made was not at any rate unreasonable or excessive cannot be a ground for thinking that the decision recorded by this court in some earlier cases was incorrect and it is difficult to say why those instances which might justify a Revision of the Judicial opinion expressed before an earlier date should be regarded as insufficient to show that instances are which may justified a revision.

The appellant company was a private limited company. It had its registered office at Delhi and its branches were situated in Delhi. The Company Law Board, after considering the report of the Board, made an order under section 237(b) of the Act directing that the affairs of the company be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Central Government. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order on the ground that it violated fundamental rights of the Company and its members and other persons, and that the Board had no power to authorise the Chairman to sub delegate this function to himself and consequently the Chairman was not competent to make an order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the power conferred by section 237 (b) to an investigation and delegated by it to the Company Law board could be validly exercised by the Chairman of the appellant company, and therefore the Board was not authorised to delegate its function under section 235(b). In appeal to this Court, HELD: The discretion conferred on the Central government by section 236(b), to an order investigation and delegation by it is administrative. It can be validly delegated by the Board to the company Law Board (Procedure) Rules, 1964 made by the State Government under section 642(1) read with section 10E(5). [319 B] The discretion given to the Central Govern ment under section 236 (b), is an administrative power and not a judicial function. It cannot be delegated to any authority or body of persons subordinate to it. The power conferred on it by section 235 (b)(ii) is administrative in nature and must be exercised by such person as he thinks fit. [320 C] In the present case, the Board could not pass an order unders. 237(a), because the appellant had no authority to delegate the function of the Chairman. The Board was acting under section 234(b)(i) readwith section 10F(5) and therefore it could not be said that the exercise of the power did not violate any fundamental right of the respondent company, or its members.

The appellants were tried and convicted for the same offence and received a like sentence. The trial court acquitted them under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code but reduced their sentences to one year ' rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence of the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the presumption in the case of dacoity was established because dacoity was proved; (ii) the fact that the accused were dacoits would not have been sufficient to bring home the charge under section 411 of the Code, and (iii) the prosecution had failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellants were dacoits. HELD : The conviction was correct in all the circumstances of the case. It is only when the accused can be connected with the crime itself that the presumption may be drawn under section 114 of the Evidence Act but not have the lesser presumption. [723 B] (i)(ii) In the present case, the appellants had been convicted on the sole evidence of having in their possession pieces of cloth which were later identified to belong to the traders. The presumption was stronger when the discovery of the stolen goods was made immediately after the crime is made immediately before the offence. [823 C] (iii)(iv) In some cases there may be other elements which may be found, but small, the finding of the theft property with a particular accused. It must not be forgotten that in some cases it may be possible to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of receivers of stolen property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [825 E] (v) The presumption under section 412 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not a rule of law but it is only a rule that the burden of proof lies on the accused to prove his innocence. In this case, there was no other evidence to show the complicity of the persons in the crime.

The petitioners were manufacturers of 'thinner ' within the meaning of Rule 2(x)(2) of the Rules. The petitioners, who are manufacturers of "thinerner" in their respective States, filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for quashing the validity of Section 5 of the (12 of 1919) (hereinafter called 'the Act '). The petitioners contended that the provisions were ultra vires and arbitrary power to the State Government to include any substance as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale and sale of the specified poison. The petition was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal, this Court held that the Act is not violative of Article 14 of the Consti tution of India. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Act is intended to regulate the possession and sale, whether wholesale or retail of poisons kept for sale by any licence holder under these rules (except those kept for Sale by a chemist, druggreen) and that is not in dispute. [225G] 2. The object of the enactment is to regulate, possess and sell the specified medicine which the Govern ment consider its possession for sale or sale to be regulat ed in the interest of health and safety of the society. It is those substances which the Government considers its possession to be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the possessed sion thereof desirable. [226H] 3. The provisions are intended to prescribe a rule or notification issued under the Act for sale, and the sale of specified poison in a Rule or notification made under the Rules including other substances to the list of substances included in the Rules as 'Poisons ' is not automatically made applicable to the other States. [227A] 4. The power vested in the State Govern ment to amend the same by rules including other substance which the percentage of such soluble material does not exceed 30% of such Soluble materials is not automatic and regulated. It was a law in force in the territory of India before the commencement of the constitution and as such continued in force. [228B C] 5. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as 'poisons ' within Rule 2 (x)(1) which has been declared as poison is not necessarily made applicable. It may be that some substances are included in a rule, notification or notification under the act but they would include only those substances specified in the rule or notified under the acts. [229C] 6. The expression "poisons kept" in Rule 2 means any substance which is specified as poison in any local area in which the use of such poison for purposes of committing murder or mischief poisoning by cattle appears to it to beof such frequent occurance as to make restriction on its possession. It does not include the substances which are specified in Rule 3(x) of Rules. [230D] 7. The word "poison" is used in a restricted sense and includes all forms which are included therein. The words "thins and methods of packing" in the definition of 'poison ' are not defined in the Act. It has been defined as to include the substance specified in a notification or order issued under this Act. [231B C]. 8. The use of the word "political" in a restrictive sense is not confined to the form of poison. It means that it must be used for the purposes of preparing, publishing and selling any substance. The term "poppy" has been used in the wider sense in which it is used as a device to make the substance known as poison. [232C D] 9. The definition of "polyan" in section 2(xi) of Act 1/1904 was omitted by substituting the old Rule 13 and consequential amendment of rules 12 and 13 of the Poisons Rules, 1926.

The assessee firm, a registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, carried on business at Madras in drugs, chemicals, mercury, camphor and silk yam. The assessee firm applied to the tribunal under section 66(2) of the Indian income tax Act for the recovery of the amount due from the Bombay firm as bad debt representing loss sustained in the other business. The Tribunal rejected the application but on appeal, the High Court held that the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ was not one incurred in the course of money lending business and that the transaction in the account of the assessee firm was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending assets. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the Revenue that the amount of Rs., 2,67,385 was not an "accommodation" within the meaning of section 10(2)(xi) of that Act. HELD : (i) The High Court erred in disallowing the debt on the ground that the debts were due in respect of the business of the appellant other than money lending. [844 C] (ii) The amount of interest, if any charged and a summary of the orders made by the Income tax Officer, the failure to adjust interest in the accounts of the Bombay Firm at the stage which it became a debtor in Samvat Year 2007, was not considered at all, and the Tribunal rejected that application. [820 D] (iii) The fact that the sums in question were not sent to the Bombay firms as loans made in the ordinary course of their business would not make any difference in the position in regard to the amounts due at the end of each year at the foot of the account, and it was an "incommodation" which could be said to have been made by a firm in the normal course of its business. [821 E] (iv) The Tribunal was right in holding that the loans were not made in ordinary course Of the money lending asset but a debt representing losses sustained in other business of assessee.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that as the awards in these cases had not been made within two years from September 20, 1984, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same amounts also amounts to suppression of material facts. [501B] 2.2 The interim order passed by this Court shall be excluded. It is well settled in law that the relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so, his application is liable to be dismissed. [601C] 2.(a) The interim stay orders have no direct bearing upon the question of the existence or non disclosure thereof amounts to concealment of material fact. [401D] (b) The relief under article 136 of Constitution is not discretionary and the petitioner who approached this Court seeking such relief should come with full disclosure and complete facts. He does not suppress any material facts, nor suppresses material facts which he has suppressed or so suppresses. The Government of West Bengal, in exercise of its powers under section 3(1) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, issued a notice to the Taj Group of Hotels for the construction of Five Star Hotel. The Government of India, however, did not give any reply to the said notice and filed an application before the Controller of Estate for permission to construct five Star Hotel on the ground that the Zoo could not be run for a single day without the essential services which were being provided in the four acres of land proposed to be given for the hotel. The Controller of Estates, however granted permission to the Stall Group of hotels to start a Five Star hotel. On appeal by the Taj group of Hotels, the Division Bench held that the decision to lease the Begumbari land to the Government of the State was based on the assumption that the view taken by the Government in taking a particular action was not unreasonable or arbitrary and that taking away of four acres from the Zooo would interfere in any manner with the animals in the Zoological Garden. The Division Bench, however held that there was no justification for holding that the construction was neither unreasonable nor arbitrary. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was not justified in proceeding on the basis that the land which was undoubted could interfere in a manner with its animals in Zoo and the removal of the burial ground and dumping ground for rubbish. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The approach which we have mentioned at the outset is one of the exceptional cases where the State has made available to this court all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of the land proposed by the Govt. in favour of the Government. [263B C] 2.1 The yardstick of price in public interest or interest, but in a case like this where the state is all that is needed to be taken into account by the government in formulating its policies and it is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Government In taking a certain action, there would be no question of any resin being sold in the open market. [264D] 2(a) The principle of "public interest" has to be applied in all cases where public interest is involved. It is not necessary that the State should know what is needed for the public good or for public good. [265E F] (b) In a case where the Government is all along interested in setting up industries within the State, it may not be possible to say that it wants a particular industry to be set up within the state and invite those interested to come up with pro posals for the purpose.

The assessee, a partnership firm, carried on money lending business in the name of his son. The Income Tax Officer held that the sum of Rs.67,560/12 was rightly included in the net wealth of the assessee. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that it was not necessary to make any gifts aggregating to the amount gifted to the donee and gift in such case would not constitute delivery over the gifted property to the donor and gift could not be valid. The High Court also held that there was no valid gift on the date of the entries, and that the assessee did not make any valid gifts aggregating Rs.1,50,000. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the assessee that the amount of Rs.,67, 560/12 could not constitute a valid gift because the assessee had made a valid gifts of Rs 1 lakh and Rs.50, 000 in his favour and the gift of Rs 25,000 made in his name and the gifted of Rs 50,000 was rightly excluded from the net assets of the assesses. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Courts were right in holding that the amounts gifted to a donee would not form part of the property passing on the death of the donor. [130D] (2) The assessee had a credit amount with firm or with family or with a banking company and that sum was available to that firm or company which carried on moneys lending business also. It was held on the facts of that case that there were no valid gifts worth Rs. 1,50 ,000 made by the deceased to his son and to his wife respectively. [131E] (3) The gift was held to be invalid because the amount was not available with the firm or the family or a company which was not a banking Company or which had no overdraft facility by mere book entries might be possible but where a sum was not present with the family, then a valid Gift by book entry might be reasonably possible but when a sum is not available to the firm, it resulted in a valid transfer even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would effectuate a valid purchase. [132F] (4) The fact that the money was transferred by further entries in the books of account of the firm would not make no difference because the transaction was genuine and there was an agreement to sell. [134G] (5) The amount gifted was not received back by the donor but was credited in the personal account of his wife, and the gifts were held to have been made contemporane ously shown that the transaction had been made Yours propor tive.

The appellant, a District Judge and the Registrar of the Orissa High Court, was posted as district judges. On October 10, 1966, he was transferred to the State of Orissa. The appellant challenged his transfer order by way of writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed on November 10, 1967. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the High court had no authority to act as law secretary, deputy law and superintendent; (ii) the Registrar was not competent to transfer a district judge from one post to another; (iii) the power to transfer an advocate was always exercised in consultation with the High Courts and by large and on the recommendation of the High. Court the transfer order was always exercise in consultation and the High, Court had no power to fill up any of the posts in the secretariat; (iv) the transfer of judicial officers working in the Secretariat was not justified because the appellant was transferred from one cadre to another. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: The High Court was within its powers in posting Shri B.K. Patro, district and sessions judge, Bolangir, Bolongir, District and Sessions judges as deputy secretary to government in law department, deputy Law and superintendent. [626 C] (v) The power to make transfer of a district Judge from one place to another is vested in the Governor and not with the transfer or posting to the cadre which power is vested by article 235. [727 D] (vi) The High court has power to direct transfer of judges already appointed or promoted or posted to the cadres which power was vested in it by article 236. [828 E] (vii) The State Government has already implemented that part of the order as well.

The appellant, a co sharer in the suit land, was allotted to one of his sons. The respondent 's father died leaving behind two sons and three daughters. In the partition suit filed by the appellant, the respondent claimed pre emption under section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Preemption Act, 1913 on the ground that he had not been co sharers in the family property or sold or a part thereof. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1) (f) and (g) of article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the suit property belonged to more than one co sharner, he was entitled to claim pre emptption under clause (a) and therefore, entitled to assert his right of pre emplption under clauses (1)(b) and(g). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'other co sharators ' in section 15 (1) is wide enough to include all co sharERS who do not fail under clause(a) even if they happen to be co share. [127B C] 2. The word 'other sharers ' in clause (b) of section 15 has been used in the first three clauses of section 18 which are meant to serve as residuary clause to ensure that no co sharee is a co holder and can exercise the right of preemption conferred on him by that provision. [128D] 3. The object of the Act is to provide for pre em plption of co sharors in the joint land or property, and to enable them to enjoy the benefit of pre ent emption. It is not necessary that all co cos sharers should be co tenants jointly, only the other co shars jointly, except the other members jointly, the right to hold, acquire or dispose of property conferred by Article 19 (1). [127E F] 4. The legislature wanted to confer the right on co sharator in the father 's brother or mother 's sons or daughters 's son or daughter 's brothers or vendors in the other two clauses of Section 15(l)(b). It is seen that no Co sharer can claim pre entption while her brother or sister cannot claim pre ferption while she brother or a daughter 'S son or daughters can exercise right of post emption conferred on them by that clause. [129F G] 5. The Act was intended to serve the residuary clause in the fourth clause which was meant to serving as a residuary clause. It was not necessary for the legislature to confer this right of Pre emption on the kinsfolk. [130G H] 6. The language used in section 13(1), read with section 15, is clear and unambiguous. The intention of the legislature is clear that no cooperative sharer is left out. It cannot be said that the object of enacting the Act was to provide a co cosharers for the benefit Of pre emections. [131H; 132A] 7. The Legislature wanted to give effect to the provisions of section 13 (1), which conferred a right of ad emption in favour of co tenants, who hold under tenancy of the vendor or vendors.

The alienees had been in possession of the property from the date of the sales which was more than three years ' old. The alienees have also received the same amount under these documents. In view of the fact that a compromise petition has been filed in this Court, it is unnecessary to refer to the facts leading to the litigation. [540E F] The alienee had no interest in the property prior to the compromise and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The transferee had no right in the land to part with in view of his having accepted the document of compromise. There was also a dispute as to recording of the compromise on that receipt. The parties have been heard. The question as to whether the alienees were valid and binding the alienee has taken up by the Court and no option lay before the Court for recording of compromise is taken up. [510E F G] In view thereof, the alieners had no share in the properties prior to 21.8.1987 between the father and his two sons. The only question which was raised was whether the alienations were valid or binding. The court held that once the Court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no discretion lay before it. [542G H] In the instant case, the parties have taken such stand in the litigation and have accepted the documents of compromise to be genuine. It is not necessary to refer the facts which are relevant to the controversy. The fact that the alienors had no interests in the suit property prior thereto does not make any difference.

The appellant company was a sick industrial company. The workmen of the respondent company were dismissed from service on the ground that they had not been given any notice to show cause why their services should not be terminated. The Industrial Tribunal, however, held that the benefit of sick leave was admissible to the workmen and set aside the award of the Industrial Tribunal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant company that the benefits granted under the Act in the matter of grant of sick Leave were not available to the workers on the grounds of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness for which the spell of illness for which benefit was last paid. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant 's claim for sick leave is admissible only in the cases of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. [864C] (2) The question regarding adequacy of the sick ness benefit under the first proviso to section 49 of the Act, has been examined by the Tribunal with reference to the reports of the National Commission of Labour, 1969, the Labour Laws Review Committee and the Norms Committee of Gujarat State, which go to show that the treatment of sickness benefit was not available. The Tribunal had also referred to the report of the Norths Committee of the Supreme Court of India, which went to show the medical opinion of the Medical Board that the said treatment was not adequate. [851C D] (3) The appellant company has been given an opportunity to show why its services should be terminated and if it is so desired, it would be entitled only in case of actual physical sickness certified at an interval of not more than 15 days. This procedure would have been followed by the Industrial Tribu nal. [874D] (4) The Industrial Tribun al has not given any opportunity to the appellant to show how their services were terminated. It is, therefore, clear that the workmen had not suffered any loss for the first two days of sickness. [885E F] (5) The fact that the workers did not deserve anything more than sickness benefit for the second two days also does not make them entitled to the benefit for an initial waiting period of 7 days in the garb of sick leaves. [891F G] (6) The workmen were not entitled to any other benefits admissible under the provisions of any other enactment. They had no right to claim any additional privilege. [902D E] (7) The contention that the sickness benefit would be lost for the next two days is not acceptable. It was not necessary in the circumstances of the case to award the benefit to the workman. This was obviously under a mistaken impression of the sickness benefits which the Act allowed for, as has been shown, as had been allowed for the earlier two days. [911F] (8) The claim for special privilege leave cannot be categorised as privilege as leave, by its very nature it would not be admissible only to the caseof actual sickness benefit and does not, at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his normal wage wages because he has been denied all the benefits. [921F H] (9) The first proviso of section 49 is intended to protect the workmen against sickness benefit which is not available in the present case. It does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit. This is obviously under mistaken impression that the sick leave has been allowed to the employees on full pay and dearness allowance in 1958, subject to the condition that the period would cease to apply when the benefits of the scheme become available to them. Such a leave could not be categorisedas privilege as Leave, by itself, it will be admissible even in the ease of actual illness certified by registered medical practitioners.

The appellant was detained under section 3 of the Bombay Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1946. The grounds of detention were served on him on the 8th June, 1955 and he was informed that his activities had been carried on by the Portuguese authorities and that he would be arrested only after a period of one month from the date of the order of detention. He challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that the grounds furnished in the grounds were vague and not specific and no particulars of the activities alleged to have been carried out by him had been received by him or made available to the Portuguese Government. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) It is well settled that a person who has been detained under an order of preventive detention cannot be deprived of his constitutional right of making a representation against the order. [391 E] (ii) The grounds furnished are vague and do not contain any particulars of those activities which relate to the alleged vagueness of the grounds. They are, therefore, vague and cannot be said to have affected the constitutional right to be furnished particulars under article 22(6). [393 F G] (iii) It was not in public interest to disclose these details. The fact that the appellant had made a representation to the State Government did not justify his action. He could not be deprived merely because he had made an application for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act. [393 E F] (iv) It cannot be held that the order was mala fide and that such mala fides had to be imputed in a case where no particulars were at all furnished. The mere fact that some particulars are mentioned in the ground were not sufficient to justify the action taken by the detaining authority, would not vitiate the order as to the mala fides of the exercise of the power.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Army. He was dismissed from service by an order dated April 9, 1959, on the ground that he had been found guilty of misconduct under r. 14 of the Army Rules 1954. The Central Government ordered his removal from service on the grounds that r.14 of the Defence Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the . The respondent challenged the validity of the order by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that r 14 of Army Rules, 1955, including r. 15 of the Indian Army Rules was ultravires the provisions of the Act and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. HELD: (i) The two sections 19 and 45 of the were mutually exclusive. They are mutually exclusive and they cannot be read together. [451 C] (ii) The words "subject to the provisions" occurring in section 19 of the read with r. 16 of the Rules, are not ultra vires. The two Sections 19 and 30 make it clear that there should be rules providing for the removal from the service of persons subject to this Act. [452 D E] (iii) The Central Govt. has thus no power to remove a person from the services. Rule 14 is such a rule. It speaks of removal of a person subject to the Act. Rule 15, therefore, clearly provides that there may be a valid rule providing for removal from services under section 19 and the Central Government has thus exclusive power to make rules for the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions.

The appellant company was carrying on business in the manufacture of tea. It had imported tea from outside the limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale therein and at such rates as may be decided by it but not below the minimum and not exceeding the maximum rates specified in columns 2 and 3 respectively, respectively, of that Schedule. The appellant company claimed octroi duty on the basis of the rate fixed by the Government before levying octroi under r. 21. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the octroi duty was validly levied by the Panchayat as it had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The rule which authorises the levy of octroi from April 1, 1963, relates back to April 1. 1963 and the period of sixty days commences from the date of publication of the notice under r., 4 i.e., the date which shall be specified in the notice. [222 B C] (ii) The Municipal Committee was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits. The Standing Committee inspected the premises of the company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea is crushed or processed, treated or chemically treated, chemically treat and treat chemically treating chemically. [223 C] In the instant case, the Standing Committee visited the premises and found that the resultant product was completely different from the tea imported into octroi limits of Panchayat for use or consumption therein. The Municipal committee did not consider whether the Tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically so as to convert it into a marketable commodity. [224 D] (iii) The High court may remand the case to the Panchayat Samiti or deal with it as it may consider best in accordance law. [225 B C].

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the . The District Magistrate, Dhanbad in respect of the petitioner 's activities were prejudicial to maintenance of public order. The petitioner challenged the detention on various grounds including that he had been falsely implicated and was not at all concerned with the murder; that the detaining authority had confirmed the order of detention without application of mind and without considering the relevant documents referred to and/or relied on, and therefore, the continued detention of the detenu was illegal. The District Judge rejected the petition holding that the petitioner was in jail and was entitled to be released forthwith. In appeal before the High Court it was contended that the order was made on one incident relating to exchange of fire between two rival groups; that there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record, and that the detention order was necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The detaining authority was satisfied that his release from one prison to another was imminent and the order passed was not on proper consideration. [910C] 2. The order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in custody and there was no possibility of his being released or that there were such a possibility of their release. In these circumstances, therefore, while the actual order of the detention was served upon the detenu, the matter of service of the impugned order under the Act on the petitioner and other factors which could justify the detention of a person is in jail, and there is no indication that either the prospect of immediate release or that the prospectof his imminent release was properly considered by the detaining Authority properly and with seriousness consider by the Advisory Board properly and seriously before the service of such order. [1011D E] 3. The detenu has been detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 on the ground that he was in custody of that there had been indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendlity business of coal to establish the criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers and passers by of the area. [1110F] 4. The detention order passed by the District Magistrate is, therefore set aside. [1211D] 5. The petition is accordingly allowed. The respondents are directed to be set at liberty forthwith.

The appellant, a dealer in gold was granted permission to carry on business as a money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises. The appellant was permitted to carry out his business in gold and ornaments. In the course of its business, he carried on business in silver. He was also allowed to carry it on by way of loan from the Government. On the question whether the appellant had suffered from excessive delegation of legislative power, HELD: (1) Section 28 confers an arbitrary uncanalised and uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at the mercy of the Administrator while granting permission or renewing a license to a dealer. The object of putting the Act on the statute book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and use of, gold and articles of gold and article of gold ornaments and articles thereof connected therewith or incidental thereto. [1154B C] (2) The object in putting the statute on the Act is to provide, among other things, for control of the production, sale, manufacture or supply of, sell, use or possession of gold, gold ornaments, jewellery and articles etc. in business as money lender, banker or any other business in the said premises. [1054D] (3) The word 'region ' is not decisive of the matter. It does not impose any blanket or uncanalised powers upon the administrator when he chooses to negative the request. In other words, the restrictions that have been put on the activities of the traders doing business in Gold will have to be viewed from the aforesaid perspective. [954D E] (4) The purpose of putting section 28 of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the . is to afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his power. [855E F] (5) The objective, the policy and the scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the Scheme affords sufficient guidance for the Administrator to exercise his discretion under section 5(1) of the Gold Control Act.

The appellants, who were the trustees of a Hindu temple, filed a suit against respondents 1 to 3 for possession of certain properties. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit. In appeal by special leave it was contended that (i) the transfer made by the manager of a religious endowment in regard to which the alienees had been acquired by adverse possession prior to 1 1929, was void ab initio; (ii) the transfers were not retrospective in operation and that if the title of the alienee in regard thereto had been transferred for valuable consideration, it would not be affected by the provisions of article 134 B. HELD: (i)(a) The transfer made in favour of the manager by a previous manager was void as being contrary to article 134B of the Constitution. [419 C] (b) The alienor was still alive and so, he dealt with the property belonging to the religious endowment. If that be so, there is no escape from the conclusion that more than 12 years have elapsed since the date of removal of the previous manager who transferred the properties in question; and so if a suit were brought by respondents 1to 3 on the basis that it belonged to the temple de facto, the possession of the transferee was adverse to the Hindu religious endowment from the very beginning. [442 D E] (ii)(a). The transfer was for valuable considerations which would govern the application of limitation in the said article which alone could exclude transfers made by a manager of the temple. If the alienor had been removed from office by other persons who were acting as de facto managers of the religious endowments, the transfer is void abitio and the possession was adverse from the date when the transfer was effected.

The respondent No. 1, a theatre owner of the Apsara Theatre, was granted a licence for exhibition of cinematographs in the building known as Apsarara Theatre. The District Magistrate rejected the said application on the ground that it had become impossible for him to operate the Cinema licence in view of the temporary injunction issued by the District Magistrate. On appeal, the District Judge held that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any other party except the original licensee, namely, Shri Ved Gupta and six of the partners who were residing with him from interfering with him. The High Court set aside the order of the District magistrate and directed the suspension of cinema theatre. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the licensing authority had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order, and that the impugned order was void and in violation of the principles of natural justice. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The licence granted by the district Magistrate is not a license but only a licence. [882C] 2. The licensing authority has no power to suspend a licence under the provisions of the Act and the Rules for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the licences and answerable to the licensing authorities for all commissions or omissions in the Cinema premises, he may be saved from any prosecution or other action under law in the capacity of licensee of the theatre owner. [ 882F] 3. The only other reason stated by the High Court for quashing the District Magistrates ' order is that under the Provisions of the and the rules for due observance of all the conditions mentioned in the licence, the licensing Authority had no jurisdiction to suspend the cinema theatre and therefore, the impugned orders passed by the said authority were void and illegal. [820G H] 4. The fact that the licence was granted to Shri Ved GUPTA in his individual capacity or as representing the partnership cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. [821H; 882A B] 5. The order passed by a District Magistrate directing suspension of the cinema shows in the Theatre shows in his personal capacity or in the names of the firm Apsa Theatre was being conducted by some persons other than the licensee, and hence the licence had been suspended.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain properties, leased to them for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. The respondent issued a notice to the appellants under section 12 of the Act as evacuee property, and under section 8(1) of the , they became vested in the Custodian for the State. The appellants filed an application before the Custodian claiming that the lease should be cancelled and why they should not be evicted. The Custodian rejected the application on the ground that the respondent had no authity or authority to issue notice in question under section 10, and that the notice was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under that section. On appeal by the appellants, the Custodian held that the provisions of section 12 applied only to leases granted by the evacuee and not by the Custodian himself, and therefore the notice in respect of movables in respect thereof had become the property of the evacuee. The High Court on a reference held that section 12 was ultravires the powers conferred upon it by section 10 of the . On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of the Bombay Act which confer power on the Custodian to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof are unqualified and absolute. [982 C] (ii) The Custodian has the power under section 13 to cancel the lease granted by himself and not merely by the evacuees but also by itself. It is open to the Custodian, to cancel that portion of Exhibit A in pursuance of Exhibit C, that the property belonging to the evacuee was not raised in the petition, and no contentions were put forward at any stage prior to the amendment, but it was not put forward as a ground for declining to entertain it which it may be noted is that by reason of the sale, the movables had become vested in him as the Custodian. [ 982 C D] (iii) The respondent could not cancel the leases granted under Exhibit A, because the Custodian had no authority under section 11 to issue any directions with reference thereto.

The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh, was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March, 1963 and was only 13 years old when the ceiling proceedings were finalized by the Sub Divisional Officer on 5th May, 1976. The Board of Revenue held that Surendrapal Singh (appellant herein) was born in the year 1964 and was merely 13 years when the Ceiling proceedings were finalised by the sub Divisional officer on 5 th May, 1977. In pursuance of the direction of the Board, the SubDivisional Officer, Hanumangarh, made a revision application under Section 230 of the Act of 1955 before the Board of revenue. The Revenue Appellate Authority set aside the order of the Sub Divis. and remanded the case to the Sub Division Officer, Saangarh for fresh determination of the ceiling area. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order on the ground that it was not appropriate for the Board to exercise its powers under Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act of 1956 and set aside that part of the sub Divis sion. The High Court held that the State had no jurisdiction to set aside an order of Sub Divisional officer, Hanumagarh, set aside his order of remand and remanded it to the sub division Officer, Sawai Madhopur, for de novo determination of ceiling area for the appellant in law. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High court was not justified in setting aside the orders of the Revenue Appellate authority and remanding the case back to the Board for fresh adjudication of the revision application filed by Raghubir Singh. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The power of superintendence and control over all revenue courts is vested in the State Government under Section 220 of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Code. It is a well settled principle that the powers of superintendence conferred on the High Courts are not subject to any other provisions of the Constitution. [775F] 2.1 In the instant case, the Board had by its order dated 14th April, 1975 directed that the ceiling areas may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1954 and not according to new law i;e. Land Revenue Appellate Authorities under Section 221 of the Government of India Act, 1915. The order of reference was made on 5.5.1976 and remanded to Sub Divisional Magistrate, Hanumatarh for de re novo determination. [875F G] 2(a) It is clear from the language of section 221 of Rajasthan Land Reforms Act of 1935 that the Board has general powers of supervision and control of all revenue Courts. In the Government Of India Act of 1915 there was provision under Section 224 for superintendence by the High courts 's superintendence and management over all Revenue Courts. The State had general power of supervision, control and supervision over all subordinate revenue courts and it did not apply to judicial proceedings. [754A B] 2.(b) It was clear from section 221 that the board of Revenue has general power to superintendence and administration over all revenues courts. In view of the fact that the Boards of Revenue had general powers to superintendence, control, supervision and management of revenue courts, it didnot apply to Judicial proceedings. The sub division officer, Sub Divisional Judge, Hanumgarh, was not competent to exercise the powers conferred by section 9 of Land Revenue (Amendment) Act of 1976. [75F H] 3.(c) It could not be said that the power conferred by Section 9 was limited to executive control and superintendence of the revenue courts. The Government of Rajasthan had general jurisdiction over all judicial proceedings, but it did so because the Board was competent to make use of its powers of control and management. [751A B; 875C] 4.(d) It cannot be said in view of section 224 that the control and administration of the board over revenue courts vested in a State Government.

The appellant, a newspaper company, was engaged in the business of printing and publishing newspapers. The first respondent, a news Reporter, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the . The High court held that the 'newspaper ' was not a newspaper because according to it, the law report published by the Ist Respondent contained information about the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are public bodies and these matters were in which the public is interested. Hence it was not necessary for the first respondent to publish the said law reports. The appellant filed a special leave petition before this Court against the decision of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Act does not carry any news and that the public are not interested in them. [782C] 2.2 The Act is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of newspaper establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provision of the statute, one opinion may not occupy a substantial part of a law report to make it a newspaper. [882D] 2(a) The Act in question was a beneficient legislation which was enacted for improving the condition of service and as such the order made by the Central Government on the basis of recommendations of Justice Palekar Award was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. [783B C] 2.(b) The law reports published by Ist respondent contain information about recent events, comments on them etc. They are binding on all the courts throughout India.
