They were binding on every court throughout India and hence neither the publication of these items nor the news report is sufficient to make a law Report a newspaper which may cease to be a newspaper and become a book. [784C D] 3(c) The Central Government was not competent for the Legislature of the State of Orissa to levy sales tax on the sale of Cuttack Law Times, which according to them were published by it. [781D E] 4.(d) The High Courts in India are vested with the power to levy tax on sale of any newspaper. But the Act does no say that the publication is not a mere paper. It only provides for publication of the said matters. [780E F] 5(e) The word 'newpaper ' has been defined by section 2 (b) and it was also not essential for a newspaper to conform strictly to the usual pattern of a daily or weekly newspaper which members of the public ordinarily read in order to get reports of recent events. [779C D, G] 6(f) The expression 'new paper ' is used in the Act as meaning newspapers only. It is significant that the expression 'Newspaper" is defined by Section 2 (c) and its publication may not have a substantial portion of a Law Report to make the newspaper a law reports to make them a newspaper, the publication whereof may not hold a substantial Part of a statute report.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent filed an application for eviction under section 21(1)(a) of the Bombay City Tenants ' Act, 1949 on the ground that he was in occupation of the premises on 1st February, 1973 and that the licensor had agreed to allow him to occupy the said premises subject to certain conditions. The appellant resisted the application contending that he had been inducted as a monthly tenant of respondent and that he could not be evicted by the respondent without notice under section 22(1) (a). The Small Cause Court rejected the contention of the appellant and held that the respondent was a licensee and not a sub tenant. The High Court allowed the revision on the view that the appellant had failed to prove that he is a tenant and having found that the period of licence had come to an end, he passed an order of eviction against the appellant. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in interfering with the finding of the Small Cause court that the licence was not put an end to by the appellant as a mere licence and that in any event by filing the application for the eviction he had granted an implied licence to the respondent licensee to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The agreement would be construed not as merely a licence but as a lease. [2181 D] 2.1 In view of the fact that the parties had agreed with the landlord and having regard to the nature of the documents, the agreement would not be construed as mere licence but a lease and not as a licence. [2282 C] 3.2 The agreement was not a lease but as an interest in the property, the contract would be interpreted as a simple licence but it was a licence and not an interest. [2383 D] 3(a) In view thereof, the High court should exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution. [2682 C E] (b) The agreement is not a mere lease but a licence as a license but as licence. It is a licence which is coupled with an interest and in the premises, the agreed consideration would be clearly construed as a sale of good deal. [2783 D F] 3.(c) In the instant case, the respondent had given an implied license to the appellant for carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years from 1st September, 1965 till 31st March, 1966 and it was also a licence that was not given effect to by him. The lease agreement would therefore be construed to have been executed in favour of the landlord. [2583 D E] 4.2 In view Of the fact the respondent has failed to establish that after 31st May, 1966 the appellant was in possession of the suit premises on the 1st of February, 1974 as there was nothing on record to show that after 30th March, 1967 the respondent licensor had granted a implied licence. The plea of the appel lant that he being a tenant, and having held that he would be a licensee, the tenancy agreement would also be construed cannot be accepted. [2483 E] 3:1 The agreement in question was not an agreement for leave and licence but an interest therein. It was a lease which was coupled with a landlord and not to the tenant. There was no estoppel against the respondent and there was no equity. [82F G] 4:2 In the present case, it is clear from the evidence that after 1st May 1966 the respondent inducted the appellant in possession as a licensee. The licence was renewed or any fresh agreement was entered into. It could not therefore be said that there was any estoppel against him. [83G H] 3 :3 The High court had rightly held that since the respondent did not plead that he became a tenant under the tenancy, the suit was maintainable. [84C D] 4(a).

The appellant was a company incorporated in the United States of Patiala and East Punjab. The Ruler of Pepsu became the Ruler of the former Jodhpur State of Patiala, and the latter was the Ruler thereof. On August 1, 1950, the Ruler passed an order under section 3(1) of the Merger Agreement whereby he agreed to pay certain sums of money to the Ruler for the continuance of the laws in the covenanting State till the date of the merger. The appellant filed a suit against the Ruler and the Ruler contending that the liability of the latter to refund the amount of tax collected by him was not discharged by the Ruler, but only by way of an act of State which was an act or agency of the Ruler. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the Ruler had no authority to confer any right on the appellant and that the suit was barred by article 295(2) of Schedule VII of the Constitution. On appeal, the High Court held that the agreement was not a law within the meaning of article 295 (2) Of the Constitution and that it was not enforceable by citizens against the new sovereign as it was part of the Covenant which had come into existence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The agreement was neither recognised by the new State of Pepsu nor was it enforceable by the appellant. It was a law made by the successor State of Punjab in respect of the rights and liabilities of the old Ruler of Patiala State. [184 D] The agreement continued until they were repealed or altered. The liability to refund any amount collected in advance for the continuation of the existing laws, after the merger, ceased to exist and the liability may disappear provided the new law was within the competence of the State legislature and did not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force.

The appellant, a market committee, was constituted under the provisions of the Madras Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1939. The appellant was a trader in the business of selling and selling agricultural crops. He had been granted a licence to purchase and sell the commercial crop in the State of Madras. On the question whether the allowance described as 'a trade allowance ' was a trade allowance within the meaning of section 14 of the Act, HELD : (i) The word "mahi" in section 14(1)(d) means a trade allowances or a trade charge which is charged on goods bought and sold by a trader. It does not include trade allowances but includes trade allowances. [109 G] (ii) The appellant had two fundamental rights: one was to carry on trade or business and the other was to hold their property, i.e., the market committee. He could only do so if he did not use the goods for any other purpose. But if he used them for a particular purpose, he would be entitled to do so under section 14. [110 A C] (iii) The bye law does not prohibit the deduction of trade allowance and does not operate upon any other payments which are not trade allowances; it merely provides that trade allowances should be paid in respect of commercial crops. If the payment is de hors the terms of the transaction but made towards consideration for the use of the premises or services rendered, it would not be a deduction from the price or commodity agreed to be paid or transferred. [111 D E] (iv) The question whether mahimai ' was trade allowance or not depends upon the nature of that deduction. If on the other hand, mahinai ' is a trade Allowance within the definition of section 2(g), the said part of the bye law will be superfluous as the allowance falls within the terms Of the section.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to transportation for life. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The facts disclosed in the charge were not sufficient to warrant an inference of common intention in Pandurang 's case. It was not necessary that there should have been a previous enmity between the two accused and the deceased. There was no reason to depart from this practice in Pandurang. [833 C] (ii) The fact that some stick blows were found on the body of the deceased did not justify an inference that it was only a short blow. It could not be said that any particular blow had been caused by a stick or sticks. There is no reason why the High Court should have reduced the sentences of death in the case of Bhilia and Tukia. [873 E] (iii) The circumstances disclosed in this case do not warrant an infer intention in using Pandurang ' s case. The fact does not justify any inference that the appellant was a subsequent concoction and that it did not hit him. There were no compelling reasons for departing from this rule in Pandurang vs State of Bombay, [1952] S.C.R. 869, followed. (iv) The High court had erred in holding that the sentence should be reduced to transportation in these two cases mainly because of the difference in opinion of one Judge. There could not therefore be any justification for depart from the practice in this matter and so reduce the sentences.

The petitioner was appointed as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service but on 4.9.1965 he was reverted to the post of Assistant Engineer in class I service and was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.1976. He challenged that order for retirement and has claimed payment of remuneration which he would have been entitled to draw upto the normal date of superannuation. The petitioner contended that the order for retiring him was passed on 3.7.1961, while he was in officiating position and was conse quired to be retired by exercising power under Rule 56(j)(i) of Fundamental Rules. He also challenged that orders for retirement, and has prayed payment of emoluments which he could have been drawing upto the maximum date of retirement. The respondents contended that since the petitioner attained the age of 50 years on 10.2.1972 and, therefore, on the date of his order he had completed the age as 50 years, he was entitled to drawing up upto the actual date of compulsory retirement till the date the normal superannuation. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 (j) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servants in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the relevant time are in Class II or Class III service or post even when he holds a post of either class substantively or temporarily on officiating basis. [691G H] 2. The object of Fundamental FR 56(J) is not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56(i). It is obvious that a person who is in Class 1 or Class II service or posts even when his substantive post is not brought to an end by reverting the Government servant to his substantive appointment, whether substantively or temporary, on officiating capacity, may begin his service on an officiating basis or on a temporary basis. The possibility of a reversion to the substantive post from which he has been promoted on an ad hoc basis, has no right to thepost and can always be reverted to that post if any, on which he had a lien. [625B C] 3. The objective of Fundamental rule 56(f) is that officiating Government servants belonging to Class I or Class 11 service or Post may begin their service on officiating terms or on officiating or temporary basis and it is obvious, that they must substantively belong to the two classes of service orpost as a member of that service or class II service. [ 625E] 4. The intention of the rule is not decisive to the power contained under F. R. 56 (J) in the case of a Government servant in Class 11 Service or post, even though he holds an officiating capacity on an ex hoc basis. It is clear from the language of F.S. 56 that officiating government servants in Class l service or Class I services or posts are outside the purview of sub clause (i).

The appellant Corporation was a private limited company. The respondent, the Divisional Manager of Masulipatam was the concerned authority to settle the claim of the appellants and to pay the amount. The respondents filed a suit for recovery of the amount on the ground that the insurance contracted by the deceased was not accepted and as such there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation. The Trial Court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the proposal was not valid and it was not binding on the Corporation and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that there was a concluded contract of insurance between the appellant Corporation and the respondents. [353B] (2) The finding of the Trial Court that the funds were appropriated towards the premium payable by the respondent was correct and it could not be said that the Corporation had accepted the proposal. [356C D] (3) The fact that the deceased had paid the first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal if the proposal were not established and even if such a representation was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules exhibit 13 and the evidence on record in this case. [359D] (4) The Corporation was not entitled to reject the proposal on the sole ground that it was a matter of fact accepted by the Divisional Office. [358E] (5) The appellant Corporation had failed to establish that the first amount was appropriated towards premium payable and the said amount was paid back to the Corporation without any demur or qualification and that in any event the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality if any, if any.

The appellant company was a private limited company. It had its registered office at Madras and its branches in Madras. The appellant company had its business at Madras. In the year 1965, it entered into an agreement with the respondent company for the purchase of certain goods from the respondent Company. The respondent company agreed to sell the goods to the appellant company on payment of a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ . The appellant paid a sum in advance and the respondent was also given a receipt for the same. The agreement provided that the respondent would pay the balance amount within 15 days from the date of delivery of the goods. The contract was not terminated by the respondent on the ground that the appellant had failed to deliver the goods within the stipulated time. The trial court held that the suit was not maintainable because the respondent had failed in its duty to deliver goods within a reasonable period and dismissed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that an order granting interim injunction "is a final order" within the meaning of article 133(1) (a) of the Constitution and it was not open to the court to grant the certificate. The High Court also held that in view of the decision of this Court in M/s Benaras Bank vs BenarasBank, ; , the expression "final order" in article 133 (1) of Civil Procedure Code means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression 'final order ' in section 205(1 ) of the Government of India Act, 1935, means a final adjudication by the Court of first instance, whether the order finally disposes of the rights of the parties within this jurisdiction or not. HELD: (i) The word "final" in section 206(1)(a) is used in the context in which it occurs a final decision on the rights and obligations of the party in dispute in relation to the suit or proceeding from which appeal has arisen, is not a judgment or decree but an interlocutory order. It does not necessarily mean that the final decision must be final. [712 E] (ii) The expression "decree" in the section means an interim order which is essentially an interlocutory one and if the decision finally disposes off the rights or obligations of parties, it amounts to final decision without finally determining the rights, liabilities and obligations between the parties for determination in the suit, proceeding or proceeding. [813 G] (iii) The test of finality, according to the Court, is whether the decision ultimately disposes of a right or liability of the other party in relation thereto in dispute, in a suit or proceedings from which an appeal has been arisen, was not final. It would be a final determination within the scope of article 136(1).

The respondent company was manufacturing grey cloth in the hands of the processor. The processed fabric was sold by the processor to the processor on payment of excise duty at the factory gate. The processor 's factory was assessed to excise duty under Item No.2(a) of the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. The respondent company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment order contending that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of grey cloth plus the value thereof and manufacturing expenses which would be either included in the price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable values of the grey cloth or manufac turing profit and expenses; that the valuation of the fabric would not be the price for processing the fabrics; that there was no justification for the respondent company to charge any duty on the grey fabrics manufactured by it; that in view of the fact that the processed fabrics were sold by processor, the respondent Company had discharged its liability to pay excise duty on such goods and the value at which they would be sold was Rs.30, being the value as sessable value; that since the processed cloth was sold for processing, the price of grey fabric would have been higher than the assessable price; that even if the processed yarn was sold in the factory, the assessee would not have discharged its liabil ties under Item Nos.2 and 3 of the first Schedule to Central Excise Act, 1944; that as the processed cotton fabric had been sold for the processing of job work, the value would be Rs.20 and the manufacturing expenses would be more than Rs.5 lakhs; that if the grey fabric was not sold by him, then in such a case the value should be Rs.,30, having regard to the fact whether the processed textile fabrics were actually sold or not; that it would be appropriate to include the processor ' sessageable value. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant company it was contended that the market value of processed fabric should be the assessable valuation of processed fabrics and excise duty would be payable at the rate of Rs.60 per kg. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The assessable value would not include the processing charges and costs, expenses and manufacturing profit plus the cost of the job work done plus the manufacturing profit and the expenses. [346B] 2.2 In order to explain the position it is made clear that the declared value at the gate for the processed Fabric would be as per Rule 174 of the Central Excises Rules 1944. The price at Which the grey yarn was subjected to would give a declaration to the manufacturer as to what would be its price at the time when the processing fabric would leave the processor, 's factories plus his profit and expense. That would be, in such cases, the assessablevalue of the fabrics plus the valuation thereof and/or manufacturing expenses. That will be the correct as soresable value and manufacturing expenditure but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include processor 'Sessable Value. [347C D] 2(a). The expression "deemed factory" in Rule 174 is used in a wide sense, to mean the factory of the manufacturer who entrusts the goods to the processing machine for processing on job work basis. [348F G] (b) In order that the processor may be selling or purchasing the processed articles in the markets, it would include only the price or deemed price at what would he be selling and the said goods must be the cost at which the processed article would give declaration to him as to how would be his sale. [349C] 3(b) The expression 'deemed factory ' is used to mean a factory of manufacturer who entrusted the goods with the processing machinery for processing or processing.

The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974, he was promoted as a clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti and was confirmed as a head Clerk. The appellant challenged his absorption before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana. The writ petition having been dismissed by the High court, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Courts of Punjab & Haryana praying that he should be absorbed as a Sub Clerk in any event. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, which has been imposed upon it by the Act, rules or bye laws made thereunder or by any other law for the time being in force. [775B] 2.2 The appellant was not entitled to be absorbed in Government service as a Clerk in the Gram Panchayat until he was absorbed in the Government service. He had no right to make appointment to the post of Head Clerk. He, therefore, could not have appointed him as a sub clerk prior to June 13, 1973. [ 737B] 3.1 In the instant case, the appointment of the appellant to the Post of Head Clerks on January 21 1974 was made after June 13. 1973 when the Amending Act came into force. The appointment of respondent No. 1 as a peon in the village Lohaurru Panchayat Samitis was not recognised and protected because despite the fact that such appointment was made before June 13 1973, being the date on which the Panchayat Sam Samiti lost its power to appoint him to the said post. [875C D] 3.(a) The appellant had been appointed as an Head Clerk in a Gram Panchayat after June 12, 1973 when he was employed by the Gram Sabha until he became absorbed in government service. His appointment as a Headmaster prior to his absorption in Government Service had to be recognised and saved, despite the existence of such appointment, he could not improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after July 13, 1974 when the Panchayat sam Samiti lost their power under section 14(4) of the Amending Acts.

The appellants filed a suit for declaration and possession of the properties in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that the Amauli properties were owned by Math and the deity. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and dismissed the suit. In second appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nucleum of the Math or the deity; that the properties were held by Mahant Shivshankar Yati and not that of the deity and therefore a claim for exemption from the levy was made. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Amauli lands acquired by MahantShivshankar Yadav, Sri Thakur Yheru Yati, who owned three private properties in village Shiv Dass, were property belonging to Math or deity. The trustees died in 1917 and all those properties devolved on Mahant Shiv Shankar Yati. [663C D] (2) The position in regard to these properties was that the deity was the personal property of Mahant Shiv Das Yherali, who executed a waqf deed on November 12, 1892 bequeathing various properties to the deity, Sri Rambarakar, and that the trustees died only for the purpose of escaping personal liability to tax. [664E] (3) The High Court is right in the view that the nuvius of the dedicated property constituted the personal estate of Uma Shankar Yairi and not the deity or was the Personal property of Shivshanker Yati; that there was reason to believe that the fund from which the Amaul properties were acquired was the property belonging exclusively to Math and therefore, a claim to exemption from levy was also made. [662F G] (4) The fact that the respondent had inherited the personal properties of Uma Shanker Yati from his predecessor Shivsan Yati was not in dispute because he was granted succession certificate by the District Judge, Ghazipur in respect of both properties.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasipermanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 5 1/4 units of land in the village of Raikot in 1949. Their father Sardar Nand Singh who was 42 found entitled to quasi permanent allotment of 40 standard acres, and 15 standard acres respectively, filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that his right to quasipermanent allotments had been taken away by reason of cancellation of the allotment in their favour by the order dated October 31, 1952. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree holding that the appellants were entitled to a permanent allotment and directed the Custodian General to allot the land to displaced persons. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Custodian had no power to revise the order under section 12(1) of the Act, because, the Custodian was not competent to revise his order; (2) the notification issued thereunder was invalid as it did not give any indication as to costs and (3) the notifications were void as they were beyond the powers conferred by section 19 Of the Act. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i) The Custodian General was empowered to manage evacuee property in the compensation pool entrusted to him or it, under section 10 of the , and that property vested in him. But the consequence of the publication of the notification under section 13(1), of the 1954 Act on March 24, 1955, had become functus officio with respect to it and could not rectify any error made by him in the past. [332 C D] (ii) The power of a managing officer or a managing corporation constituted under that Act on a managing agency or a Managing corporation is vested in a managing committee or a governing corporation constituted thereunder on a full and complete basis. But, the consequence Of the publication by the Custodian, by reason Of the divesting of the property, as from March 24. 1955, has become functusofficio with respect thereto and could neither rectify any mistake made by the appellant in the previous proceedings nor could it rectify any errors made by it in the earlier proceedings. [333 D E] (iii) The provisions of sections 12(2), 19 and 19 of the Punjab Act are not inconsistent with section 10 Of the , because, they are inconsistent with the provisions of the . The Custodian was empowered under section 11 to manage the evacuee property and in exercise of his power he will be competent to allot such property to any person or to cancel an allotment or lease made in favour of a person.

The State Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Inspectress of Girls Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women 's Branch) and the advertisement inviting applications from qualified candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in the newspapers. The recruitment examination was conducted in two stages and written test/personality test. After the written examination/personature test, the successful candidates were called for interview but they were not called for the interview. On the requisition of the State Government the State Public Services Commission decided to cancel the entire recruitment process and asked for a fresh interview. The Public Service Com mission cancelled the entire selection process and directed that the order of the Public Service commission cancelling the entire examination be set aside. In appeal, the High Court upheld the decision of the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commissions to cancel all the recruitment and asking for a new interview. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The public service Commission had undertaken the recruitment to the post as Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari in Uttar Haryana Educational ServiceJunior Scale (icker) District masters of Girls School in UttarPet icates District Inspectress. The State Public service Commission decided not to cancel any written part of the recruitment examination and asked the candidates for a Fresh interview. In view of this position, when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written part, the Public Services Com mission cancelling the original part of recruitment examina tion. [125C D] 2. The High Court has upheld the action of the public Service Commission and directed re holding of the selection afresh. The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment or asking for fresh interview become final and would not be disturbed. [126E F] 3. In the instant case, the recruitment which is now to be done by completing the interview examination was over, on the basis of the two examinations and in terms of the recruit ment rules fresh selections shall be made. The process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public would not suffer.

The appellant, a Hindu Undivided Family, was the sole trustee of the Dera and was in possession of the properties attached to it. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of possession of certain properties belonging to the joint family. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no knowledge about the date of death of Som Dass and that he was in exclusive possession of those properties. In appeal, the High Court held that after the death of S, the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. The High Court also found that after his death S had died during the pendency of the suit, the interest which vested in Som Dass was the subject matter of the litigation and when a dispute is raised about such rights, then the appellant is bound to bringing on record his legal representatives. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High court should have granted leave to the appellant to prosecute the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit was for possession and management of the property attached to the D.era and its properties appertaining to it by virtue of his election as mahant. [401C] 2.1 In other cases of an assignment, creation or devolution of any interest during the pending litigation and the elected persons can be added as parties under Order 22, rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. The question whether the interest in the subjectmatter of the appeal devolved upon S was a matter of devolution of interest during pendency of a suit but that it was uncertain on the death or for any other reason. [498D] 2(a) In other words, the principle that trial of a case cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest of a party in the subjectmatter of the dispute has devolved upon another during the course of a litigation and that suit may be continued against S is not attracted. [501C D] 2.(b) The rule that has to be applied to cases of devolution or devolution does not apply to cases where there is no devolution of the interest. In other case, the right in the property devolved upon one during the period when a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of interests during the trial of the suits but that suit can be continued even if the interest is not created or retired during the proceedings of the civil court. [488E F] 2:2 The rule is based on the principle, that trial cannot be bring to an effective end merely where the interest has devolved on another during a pendency of suit but this rule is founded on the principles that trial can be brought into an end only because the interests of a person acquiring the interest with the leave of the court. When a suit may lie against a party who dies or retire during the institution of the proceedings, it is a case of devolution and there are no devolution. [487G H] 3:3 The rule in that case was not applicable to cases which arose after the filing of the present suit.

The petitioners, who were working as Assistant Teachers in the Andhra Pradesh State Higher Secondary Education Board, filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned orders of the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that the petitioners were stagnated in the lower positions due to expansion of educational facilities and that the impugned order was arbitrary and violative of Article 311 (2) of the Constitution. The State Government, however, dismissed the petitions holding: (1) that the age of retirement from 55 to 58 years was increased from 55 years to 58; (2 ) that the enhancement of the age from 58 to 60 years was not justified because it had been decided to reduce the age to 58 and (3) that there was no basis at all for reducing the age. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Government had decided to increase the age in 1976 by increasing the age between 55 to 60. It is not unreasonable or arbitrary in the circumstances of the case. [518G] 2. The proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the constitution has no relevance to the present decision of the State to reduce its age of superannuation from 58 years to 60 and that, therefore, the Government was estopped from reducing the retirement age from 55. [619A B] 3. The contention that the reduction of the date of retirement is arbitrary and unreasonable in the facts of the instant case is not hit by Article 14 or Article 16 since it is not arbitrary or unreasonable in nature. [720C D] 4. The impugned orders are therefore violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Consti tution of India. [821D E] 5. The petitioners have a right to challenge the validity, legality and validity of these orders on the ground that they were arbitrary and discriminatory. They cannot be permitted to challenge those orders as they are not in accordance with law. [422C D; F G] 6. The question whether the Government has acted arbitrarily or unreasonably is one of fact which must be determined by the facts and circumstances of each case. It would depend upon the facts, circumstances and circumstances bearing on the question of age of the retirement. [921D] 7. The power to alter the conditions of service cannot be exercised so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be amended retrospectively so as not to take away rights which had already accrued to them. [1122E F] 8.

The appellants were dealers in the State of Haryana. They were assessed to sales tax under section 5(1) of the Punjab Sales Tax Act, 1973 on the purchase of raw materials from outside the State and used them in the manufacture of goods specified in Schedule B. The assessing authority levied a tax on the purchases effected by the appellants on the ground that they had purchased raw materials for the purpose of export within the meaning of section 5 (1) (b) of Act 20 of 1973. The appellants challenged the levy of tax on these purchases and contended that the transactions were not taxable under section 9(1)(b) as they were not sales in the course of inter State trade or commerce in the territory of India within the definition of 'turnover ' in section 5 of the Central Sales Tax, 1956. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the purchases of raw material by the assessees were not charge able to tax either under section 3(1), or section 6 or section 24(3). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b), should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "disposition of goods liable to tax under Section 9" in section 9 (1)(c) must be deemed not to have used the goods for the purposes speci fied therein i.e. for the manufacture or sale of any other goods and dispose of the manufactured goods in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the inter State or in the Course of export out of the territory within the term of sub section (1). [351C D] 2. The words "or despatches the manufactured materials to a place outside the state" in clause(a)(i) later inserted with retrospective effect from 27.5.1971, which included cases where the purchase tax is payable under any other provision of this Act, there shall be levied, subject to the provisions of section 17, a tax at such rate as may be notified under section 15. [351D] 3. The word "discharge" in sub section(3) of section 9 means the sale or purchase of goods by a dealer who purchases them otherwise than through way of inter state trade or Commerce or in course of export outside the territory, within the ambit of sub s.(1) thereof. The sales are not taxable either under Section 5(3), but are found to have use the goods in the manner speci cised therein i fied thereunder i. e., for the purchase by a registered dealer for the sale in course or export out from the territory outside the territories of India. [352E F] 4. The definition includes within the definitions of ' turnover ', the purchase value of goods chargeable to tax and the purchase price of goods so chargeable to sales in any way otherwise than as by way Of sale in either manner by way o f sale in any other manner otherwise by way or otherwise than in any ways otherwise than on sale in that course. The Explanation thereto excludes from the definition the turnover which is taxable under sub section 5. [353F] 5. The goods presently in question are not laible to tax u/s 9( 1) (a) of Haryana Sales Tax and purchase price in any form otherwise than for the use of the goods manufactured by a dealers. The assessees would have had to pay tax on their sales effected by them but for a claim for exemption under section 24 (3). [353D] 6.

The appellants who were dealers in cotton yarn entered into contracts with the respondent for export of certain goods. The goods were exported by them to the buyers on shipment. The sales were not taxable at the point of time when they crossed the customs frontier and therefore, no tax was realisable on these sales. The High Court held that the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had crossed the custom barrier and thus entered the export stream, and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants (i) that the sale was not a sale in the course of export within the meaning of article 286 (1)(a), and (ii) that as the goods were not despatched by the buyer outside the State of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase by him or by a person to whom he sells the goods, the sales could be exempted from taxation under article 285(1) (b). HELD: (i)(a) The words " a registered dealer" in section 10(b) mean a registered person who has given such certificate under section 8(b), and the purchaser is not a registered dealers. [927 C] (ii)(a)(b):The word " a person" in article 286 means a registered or a dealer to whom goods have been sold by him outside the state of Bombay, and the expression " a dealer" includes a registered firm. The words 'registered dealer ' in section 8 mean a person who is not registered under the Act. [990 D] (b) The word "a registered dealer " in section 9 means a person whose principal place of business is to be transacted by him either directly or through another, and it includes a person holding a certificate under the , and the words "registered dealer" are used in section 12(1). The expression "registered dealers" in that section means a dealer who has been registered under section 10.

The respondent, a Hindu woman, was married to the appellant and his wife. The appellant filed an application for maintenance under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, before the Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance. The Magistrate held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 400/ for her maintenance. On appeal by the husband, the Sessions Judge set aside the order of the Magistrate and directed the appellant to pay Rs. 500/ as maintenance allowance for the maintenance of herself and her child. The High Court allowed the petition in revision holding that the respondent was a legally subsisting wife, dismissed the petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the absence of mutual consent decree in 1962 whereby the mehar money had been paid and all claims adjusted, and so no claim for maintenance could survive; (ii) the consent decree of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all claims then and no claim to maintenance could sustain under section 127(3)(b) of the Code. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The consent decree does not have the special statutory right of the divorcee under section 126(3) (b). [771 B] 2. Section 127(2)(b), as it is, provides for a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential provision as a capitalised substitute for the order under section125(3). The object of payment by way of mehar or ordained by custom has a reasonable relation to the object and is a capitalisation substitute for order under Section 125. If the first payment by customary payment at the time of divorce, has adequately provided for the divorce, a subsequent series of recurrent recurrent Recurrent recays does not by itself justify the claim that the amount so paid was more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. [772 C D] 3. The object and purpose of the payment is to enable the wife to live with her husband and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. The whole scheme of section 127 (3) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum organised payment by a ritual exercise rooted in the consent order read with section 127.(3)(a). [784 D] 4. Section 125(1) does not require that husband can claim under section 128(3), if one was to locate a legal ground to locate another legal ground for divorce, he has always provided for it with where the husband used the court 's mutual rights and obligations. The only purpose of payment is certified by the fulfilment of social obligation not by a ceremony rooted In custom. [785 E] 5. Section 126(1)(b). does not provide for any such contingency. It merely provides that if one has been divorced by her husband, by customary payments at the place of divorce and the mutual rights have been determined, the other is deemed to be the capitalised substituted for the decree under section 12(3); but if one is to locate an existing statutory right created as a substitute for a decree under Section 12(1), it is obvious that no husband can get any benefit under the current Code. [795 A B] 6. The respondent was entitled to an allowance. She had forfeited her claim because of divorce. She has forfeited her claims because of her divorce and she used the Court 's moral or personal law applicable to the parties when they entered into a contract to adjust their then mutual rights, as a customary discharge. [805 C] 7. The question whether the respondent is entitled to maintenance allowance under section 13(3A) does no longer arise in view of the provisions of section 125. [811 D E] 8. Section 12 (3)(c) provides for the payment of meli or ordeenage by way Of mehar, money, as customary discharge, is within the cognisance of that provision.

The appellant was a dealer in country liquor. He had bid for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction of the Country Liquor shop held on 27.3.88 and he gave the shop of Beni Country liquor to the respondent. The price was fixed at Rs.10,000/ per month. The appellant challenged the order before the Collector, Samastipur by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State Government that there were no requirement of giving prior notice to black listing of the appellant in respect of future contracts under the orders passed by the Collector and, therefore, the order directing that the appellant be placed in the black list for future contracts cannot be sustained in law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The black listing is an implied principle of natural justice that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural Justice. [869C] 2.1 In so far as the cancellation of the bid of the respondent is concerned, the State Govt will be at liberty to pass any order in accordance with law indicating the reasons therefor. But it is an elementary principle of the rule that any orders having civil consequences should be passing only after complying with the principles thereof. [ 869D] 2(a) The appellant was right. It was an implied doctrine of natural justi fic justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. But, it is a fundamental principle of law that any such order having Civil consequence should also be passed even after following certain principles of Natural Justice. The respondent is right. [820E] 2.(b) In so much as the appellant has not given any notice before blacklisting the appellant, if the Government is so entitled to do so in accordancewith law, i.e. giving the appellant due notice and an opportunity of making representation, it cannot be said that there is no requirement for giving any notice prior to black listed the appellant or giving him due notice. [821H; 869A] 2 (c) The order directing the appellant to be placed at the blacklist in respect Of future contracts, cannot be sustain in law and must be realised that black listing has civil consequence for the future business of the person concerned in any event. [822E F] 3(a). In sofar as the cancel of the bids of the appel lant is concerned the respondent was right; but it is equally an implied rule of law, that any action having civil effect should be pass only after follow the principlesof natural justice.

The appellant, a tenant in respect of the premises covered by exhibit P 1, leased out to the respondent under exhibit P1. The respondent filed a suit for arrears of rent based on the lease under exhibit D 1 and for mesne profits. The Rent Controller passed an order determining the fair rent at Rs.994 p.m. The appellant 's appeal before the Appellate Authority was dismissed by the Rent Control Tribunal, which held that the building on the land leased under exhibit A1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in respect thereof and that, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrear of rent was barred by section 12(4) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the tenants that since the subject matter of the lease was only a vacant piece of land with no title to the buildings standing on the site in item 17 (2), it was not open to the High Court to entertain a collateral attack on the validity or correctness of the order of the Rent Controller. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the landlord is a tenant or not depends upon the true nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the Rent controller under the Act and, therefore,. impliedly excluded from the purview of the civil court 's jurisdiction as well as the provisions of the . [534B C] 2.1 In the instant case, the question whether a landlord or a tenant is a ryot or not has to be determined by the rent tribunals as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them. The fact that an application for this purpose cannot lie except at the instance of a landlord and a tenant, the Rent Tribunal has to deal with this incidentally but this incidentally does not mean that the decision on the question is only the determination as to the fair or standard rent for the premises. [535C D] 2(a) The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is excluded from consideration by the courts as a substantive issue in determining what the fair Rent of the property should be in accordance with the provisions Of the Act, and that even if this relationship exists between the parties, the court of Small Causes will have to deal this incidentally. [635D E] 2.(b) The question on which the jurisdiction of civil court is excluded is only a determination as a final order that is null and void merely because one is valid until set aside, the answer has to turn on the true scope and scope Of the jurisdiction. [553E F] 3(c) In an application under section 4, the jurisdiction is excluded not merely because the question may have had to be considered by theRent Controller but that is not one of the direct issues before the Rent Controllers.

The petitioner was appointed as a Forest Officer on an integrated seniority list. He was given the benefit of seniority in the provisional list, but he was not allowed to participate in the final integration list. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the final list and the final seniority list, contending that the petitioner had been denied relief against the final inter State seniority list though he was given due opportunity to object to the provi sional list. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the concession in Shankariah 's case (supra) was not applicable to such a case and that the principle recognised in Shankakarah 'S case (Supra) was inapplicable to such cases. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the writ petition was premature as the final order of a few lines by which the petitioner 's petition was disposed of by the High court on the facts of the case was not referred to any facts of this case. [828B] 2.1 In view of the special circumstances of the present case, the principle recognized in Shanka vs G.M. Shankariarah & Ors., ; , that a person whose seniority is to be determined under section 115 of the Act must be given an opportunity to objects to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list; and if a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous consideration, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts. [829C D] 2(a) The principle recognised by Shankariasah ' s case (1) that a final list prepared under section 116 of the , should be provisional cannot be challenged in a writ court merely because it is made after the final publication of the provisional seniority list and not on any ground other than the one which was urged before the High Courts. The principle recognized by Shankarsah ' case (b) In order to establish the invalidity of the Final list on some grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. [882C D; 883A] 2.(a) It is not within the province of the Central Government to lay down what are in the principles to be adopted for purposes of equation. If a particular action is mala fides or arrived on totally extraneous and irrelevant considerations, such decision can certainly be interfered by Courts.[829E F] 3(b) The Court cannot go into the merits or otherwise of the matter. It is also not within its province of courts to laydown what are In the principles laid down in Shannoah ' 's Case (supra). [883C D E] 4.(c) The petitioner was not heard before final list was prepared. He had, therefore, opportunity to make a representation with regard to the two points urged by him. [826E F G] 5(d) The High Courts were right in taking the view that the principles of Shankariah ' S case (suplied) were applicable and that there was no justification for interfering with the final lists on some ground of invalidity.

The petitioners in both these writ petitions are manufacturers of rough and cut diamonds and polished diamonds. They were granted Additional licences on or after April 1, 1988, under the Import & Export Policy for the period 1978 79 to March 1991. The petitioners in all these writ petition challenged the validity of sub para (10) of para 218 of the Import and Export Policy 1988 91 on the ground that it was discriminatory between Export Houses and Export Houses which were issued Additional licences prior to April 1.1988, under which the petitioners had been granted Additional Licences on or before April 1 1988, on the basis of the export policy for the years 1978 79 and 1979 80. The respondents in both the writ petitions contended that sub para(10) was discriminatory since the conditions of eligibility for grant of Additional licences were to be given on the foundation of exports made during 1986 87 and 1989 88 and that the petitioners who had been given Additional Licences prior to May 1,1988, on or prior to June 1, 1990, were not eligible for the flexibilities in the import policy 1988 91. The writ petitions were opposed by the respondents contending that sub paras (10), (11) of Para 218 of Import & Exports Policy 198891 were quite different from those contained in the Import Export Policy 1985 88 and therefore they could be said to be similarly circumstanced as Export Houses who had already been granted additional licences on the strength of one third of f.o.b. value of the exports effected during 1986 89 and 1989 90, and that sub clause (10 ) of para 217 of the Export Policy was quite different than those contained under the Export Import & Import Policy 1988 88. The State Government contended that the Additional Licences issued to Export Houses prior to 31st March, 1991 were quite distinct from those containing in the Export and Export House Certificate as well as grant of additional licences for a much lesser value under the import Policy 1988 89 and therefore the petitioners could not be said that they had been denied the facilities which have been given to Export houses during 1986 88. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are also entitled to a similar relaxation. [236B] 2.2 In D. navinchandra & Co. case (supra) this Court has not laid down that Export Houses, like the petitioners, who were granted additional licence on orbefore April 1st, 1988 have to be treated at par with Export Houses while granting Additional licences under the Imports & Exports policy 1988 89. The petitioner therein had been allowed Additional Licences for a lesser value of exports effected in 1987 88 and 1989 89.

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of plastic goods, was manufacturing the same in packed condition and packing was not returnable by the buyer to the assessee. The appellant, a wholesale dealer, had supplied the containers to the respondent assessee at the factory gate for sale to the buyers. The price charged by the respondent was inclusive of the cost of packing which was the assessable value of the goods sold by it. The respondent assessee claimed that the cost should be included in the assessable valuation of the excisable goods and that the value had to be included therein, but the cost was not includible in the value of such packing. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that at the time of removal the goods were delivered from the factory packed condition, the price charged was inclusive and returnable by it to the buyer, there fore, the value has to be excluded in the valuation of excisable goods where such packing is durable nature and returnable to the manufacturer. The High Court, however, held that the secondary packing which is essential for putting the excisable article in which it is sold in the wholesale market at the place of removal was the degree of packing where the packing is returnable by buyer to a buyer to whom the goods are delivered at the premises of removal. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the word "cost" rather than "value", instead of "cost", would have to be given its ordinary meaning and not merely "cost". Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "cost of packing" in section 4(4)(d) of the Act is repugnant to the very scheme of section 4. It may be necessary in this connection to refer to the observations of this Court in Union of India vs Bombay Tyre International Ltd., [1985] Supp. SCC 87, and Union ofIndia & Ors. vs Bombay Rubber International Ltd. , [1986] Supp SCC 87. 2. The word "value" rather or "cost price" is a relative term used in section 3(4) (d)(i) of Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. It is in relation to section 4 (4)(a) of that Act that the meaning of the expression "assessable value" as interpreted before its amendment cou pled with the now well established position that the use of the word 'cost ' rather than 'value ' instead of 'cost price ' was repugnant to very scheme. [985B C] 3. The object and purpose of the levy, the meaning and purport of the words "assessability value" and returnable the manufacturer levies a charge for packing which are intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the goods manufactured on the market. The use of such pack ing is essentially incidental to bringing the excisable articles in which they are sold at the factories gate is to be taken as the assessable price if necessary, by addition to the sale price, the manufacturer levied a charge of packing when the packing was durable in nature and is returnable, by the seller to the purchaser. [885C D] 4. The purpose and object of the imposition, the words 'assessable Value ' in relation thereto would have been to be include in the price except where the container is durarable nature or returnable to a manufacturer.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo R.I. for 15 months under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court accepted the plea of the appellant that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the time of the seizure and the contemporary records. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The conviction under section 4(1) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act is not attracted on the facts proved. [337B] 2. The presumption arising under section 114 of Evidence Act cannot be said to be rebutted merely because the explanation offered by the accused is reasonable and probable. It must further be shown that the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact that the explanations offered by him are reasonable and plausible. [336C] 3. The burden resting on the accused person in such a case would not be as light as it is where a presumption is raised under section114 of Evidence act and cannot be hold to be negatived merely because, the explanation tendered by the appellant is reasonable or probable. [333D E] 4. In the instant case, the prosecution had failed even by preponderance of probability in rebutting the presumption arising out of the provision. The defence that there had been consistent explanation for the appellant was probable and probable, it must further he proved the guilt beyond doubt. [332E F] 5. The appellant had a consistent case even from the earliest opportunity that the currency notes found in his possession were the money returned by PW 1, the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the appel lant in view of the presumption arise under section4(1). [338F] 6. The prosecution had not even by cross examination of PW 1 or any other witness. It was only after the appellant had been acquitted that he could have been convicted. [342E F G] 7. In a case where the explanation given by the appeli lant is reasonable, probable and acceptable it must be further shown that he had received a sum of money which was not due to him as a legal remuneration. The onus resting on an accused person is not discharged merely because he has received a particular amount of money. [340F] 8. In this case, there fore, the appellant having a consistent and probable defence that the money was returned by him as the money had been returned by the PW 1 the prosecution could not be said t o have proved the charges beyond doubt against the appellant. The evidence of PW 2 and 6 is sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused. [341G] 9.

The appellant company was a public limited company. The respondent, an employee of the company, was employed by it as a Manager in a company and was entrusted with certain assets including the value of the assets of its company. On the question whether the company had the power to issue a process under sub section (2) against such officer or employee, the High Court held that cl. (b) of sub section 1 of section 630 must be interpreted to mean not only the present officers and employees of the Company but also to include past officers and staff of the appellant company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that cl.(b) is a beneficent provision contained in section 630, which has been deliberately enacted by the legislature with the object of providing a summary procedure for retrieving the property back to the company. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The words 'any such property of a company wrongfully obtained possession of any property of the public ' occurring in sub section(1) of section 6 are wide enough to include all past officers or employees of a Company. [175E] 2. The word 'officer ' is used in cl. 3 of section 68, which covers all past and future officers and servants of a firm. It is the wrongful withholding of such property which is wrongfully obtained by an officer or servant of a public company wrongfully withholds possession of it after the termination of his employment. [176F] 3. The expression 'any property of any company wrongfully withheld ' occurring under section 630(1)(b) refers to the whole of cl. 4, and that the words 'other than those expressed or directed in the articles and authorised by the Act ' are wide and comprehensive enough to cover all past employees and employees. [177G H] 4. The object of enacting sub section 3 is to protect the property of an existing officer or a employee of a private company wrongfully withholding possession of such properties during the course of his service, withholds the same after termination of employment. It would be rendered nugatory by cl. 5 which provides for a summary method for retrenching the property from the employer to the termination giving rise to an obligation to hand over the property to the employee giving rise thereto. [178G H; 179A] 5. The High Court was right in holding that cl (b), as it stood at the relevant time, did not apply to the existing officers and employee of an 'company wrongfully withhold possession of the property. It was the wrongful withheld of such a property which was wrongfully obtained from an officer of a corporation or employee of that company. [179G H, 179A B] 6. The question whether cl. 2 of section 70 is applicable only to the present officer and employees, is one of fact or another. The purpose of enacting subsection (1) is to provide for a speedy procedure for reprieving property of such an employee or employee either (a) wrongfully withhold it after termination or (b ) having obtained such property during the period of his appointment, withholding possession thereof after the expiry of the period mentioned in cl.(a). The object is to secure the protection of the interest of the existing officer and employee. [180G H]. 7. The language used in sub s. (1), which is an enabling provision, is clear enough to indicate that the legislature intended to provide a summary machinery for retruction of property back. It does not say that the Legislature intended to give a summary remedy for retrearing the property by providing for a quick procedure for re retrieval of property of another person or employee.

The appellant, a religious trust, was appointed by the trustees of the temple in question. The temple was managed by the founder of the Temple and the gifts were made with the object of maintenance of the worship of the deity for the benefit of the Hindu public as a whole. The founder also intended that regular Bhajan, Kirtan and worship shall be maintained and annual ceremonies and processions for pilgrimage shall be conducted by the saints in succession as the persons who are entitled to worship at the shrine of the Sansthan. The appellant was appointed as the manager of the said temple. On the question whether the temple was a public trust, HELD : (1) The temple is a private property and not a public endowment. The trustees of a temple are public trusts within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. [518 D] (2) In order to facilitate worship by the public, the founder also wanted that regular follow, Bhajan, kirtan or worship shall he maintained and Annual ceremonies and ceremonies for pilgrimages shall be performed by the Saints and the Sansthan and the endowments shall be made with objects of maintenance and continued the religious worship of deity. [618 E] (3) The founder of a public temple is intended to facilitate the worship by persons of the sect, who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of it. The intention of the founder was that regular separate Bhajan, Bhajan or Kirtans shall be held out of the shrines and the deities of the saint. [719 G] (4) The trustees are public trust within the definition of section 3(13). They are public endowments. The dedication to the public is a matter of right. It is not necessary that regular meetings should be held by the members of the family. The mere fact that the founder has been given some facilities for worship does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that the temple is private or public endowment, as the members who succeeded the one after other were neither owners nor trustees of such properties. [419 C] (5) The dedication in question was a religious endowment and not public trust. It was never treated as a private endowment.

The assessee was arrested and is being detained in jail in execution of a warrant of arrest issued under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 for recovery of arrears of land revenue. The Income tax Officer issued the recovery certificate to the Additional Collector of Bombay on the ground that the amount due under a decree had been recovered from him as if it were an arrear of land revenues. The assessee contended that the said amount was not liable to be recovered by reason of the provisions of section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 and that the same offended article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the contention must fail. The first part of section46(2), which provides for two different modes of recovery of income tax should be framed on a uniform basis, for the recovery of the arrears of revenue, is one and the same, and it is levied under a single Central Act, and yet the ultimate coercive processes for recovery differ in nature and between State and State. The second part of that section provides for different modes to adopt machinery for recovery and the recovery by way of recovery from defaulters of each State, the same mode of recovery, and the third part of the section lays down the procedure for the collection of income taxes. The two methods are equally distinct and separate. The State laws prescribe the procedure in respect of recovery and recovery of tax from defaulters and it can be done easily by suitably amending section 46 (2) so as to provide for the detention of all defaulters for the same period in all cases in all States.

The respondents were the workmen of the Port Trust. The respondents were employed by the Port Board as a casual labourer in the Bombay Port Trust and were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 10 per day for each day. On the question whether the respondents were entitled to overtime work, HELD : (i) The respondents are not entitled to any overtime work. They are not workmen within the meaning of section 2(d)(ii) of the Act. [41 G] (ii) The provisions of section 13 fix the number of hours in a normal working day and not the number specified therein. It is for this reason that a variable recess is in force at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks. The crew at the Alexandra Crew or the crew at a Alexandara Docks get a specified interval of time. [42 E] (iii) The scheme of the rule is to specify that the interval for rest in a working day is given by specifying a day in advance the hours of work in a week. It will also be noticed that the scheme of this rule is not to specify the interval of rest in any particular day. [43 G H] (iv) The rules are to specify a day and work beyond 12 hours. The rule is clear and unambiguous. There is no indication in the rule that the normal working days of work should be so arranged that inclusive of his intervals for rest, if owing to the nature of the work there is difficulty in giving the interval rest. [44 C] (v) The rule does not require that the hours should be worked beyond 12 noon on any particular date. It only means that the hour of work must be so fixed and rest shall not exceed 48.

The appellant tenant was let out on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika with effect from October 1, 1976 and the accommodation was again for the second time assessed on June 26, 1976, but the accommodation could not be said to have been completed. The suit for ejectment of the appellant tenant against the respondent was decreed by the Trial Judge and decreed the suit for eviction. In appeal before the High Court the appellant landlord contended that apart from the controversy about the date which should be the starting point for computing the period of 10 years in view of the language of Sections 39 and 40 of the Act, the appellant tenants will be entitled to protection under the provisions of Section 20 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act. The High Court allowed the revision petition set aside the judgment and decree of the Trial Court and decreed that suit for recovery of house tax. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of language of Section 39 of the West Punjab UrbanRent Restriction Act, 1949 it is clear that for a newly constructed building the provisions contained in sub section (2) of Section 2 will not apply for 10 years and therefore restriction as provided for in clause (2), Section 20 can not be attracted. [1034D] 1.2 The appellant tenant will be entitle to protection of the provisions under this Act because according to him the rights will have to be determined on the basis of the law applicable on the date of the suit, but looking to the language and context of Sections 40 and 40 it is obvious that for an newly constructed house tax the provision contained in Section 20 cannot apply. [1134D E] 1.(a) The appellant landlord will be eligible to protection as provided in Section 19(1)(f) of the U.P. Urban Rent Control Act, 1947. [1234F G] (b) The provisions contained therein are not applicable to the present case because the language used in Sections 39 & 40 is clear and unambiguous that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the provision of Section 19. [1335G H] 1(c) The High court has rightly held that the period between October 1 1976 and November 1,1976 should be computed from the date as indicated in Explanation 1 and it is thus clear that during the pendency of the proceedings in this Court 10 years have elapsed and therefore the appellant tenancy will be governed on the day of the litigation even if the matter is pending in this court. [1434D F] 2.(a). The language of section 39 of Act is clear enough that for every newly constructed residential building the provision has to be computed in the manner from the dates as indicated therein and it cannot be said that the provisions are not attracted. It is also clear that the appeal is the continuation of the case pending in the High court 10 years had elapsed even if date of completion is taken to be 1.10.86.

The respondent No. 1 was a thika tenant within the meaning of the Act as he was a tika tenant in that Act. The appellant, who was a jama tenant under the provisions of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, filed an application for ejectment on the ground that the landlord had failed to prove that the thika tenancy was not a thikika tenant and that the provisions Of the Act were not applicable to him. The Controller dismissed the application but the High Court held that the respondent No 1 was entitled to the benefit of the said Ordinance as he had been in possession of the ground floor, which was not covered by the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) section 4 of the Ordinance was prospective only and not retrospective; (ii) section 5 of the Regulation did not apply to the case because the landlord wanted to eject a thki tenant after the Act had come into force, as he could not have filed a suit but applied to the controller for an order in that behalf. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that sections 4 and 5 were prospective only. [1012 C] (iii) Section 4 of Regulation did apply to all suits pending on 21st October 1952. It was not retrospective merely because section 4 was prospective. The landlord had to establish the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3 in section 4. The controller in his turn had to deal with the matter in accordance with the provisions, of the Land Acquisition Act as amended by the Ordinance. [1001 D] (iv) Section 5 of Regulation does not apply when a landlord wished to eject thika tenants after the coming into force of the West Bengal Thika Act, 1949 as amended. The proviso to section 4(2) makes it clear that if at any time between the commencement of the Bombay Thika Land Tenancy (Second Amendment) Ordinance 1952 i.e., 21st November, 1952 the provisions in the Calcutta Development Tenancy (Third Amendment) Act, 1952 were subject to the provisions contained in the said Act as if they were an order made under and in accordancewith the provisions.
