The respondent 1, a company incorporated in the State of Madhya Pradesh, was carrying on business as a sugar factory. The appellant, a manufacturer of sugar, was assessed to tax under section 3(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, on the ground that it had contravened the provisions of section 68 and sub sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 69 of the Act. The respondent 1 filed an application before the Special Area Development Authority for imposition of property tax on sugar undertakings. The Special Area development Authorities rejected the application holding that the sugar undertaking was a declared industry under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951. The appeal to the Appellate Authority failed. The State Government 's writ petition challenging the order of the Special Authority was dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the provisions inserted in the Municipalities Act and the Municipal Corporation Acts were deemed to have come into force with effect from April 1, 1976; (2) the levy of property taxes on lands and buildings owned by or vesting in the Union Government under section 127A of the Municipalities and section 135 of the Municipal Corporations Act was not in conflict with the power conferred by the State Legislature on Special Area Planning Authorities to impose the property tax, and (3 ) that the provisions introduced in the Municipal Councils and Nagar Panchayats were ultra vires. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned Act is not in any way defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69(d) of Municipalities Act or section 135 thereof. [23D] 2.1 The State Legislature had no competence to pass the impugned Act by reason of Entry 52, List I read with Entry 24, List II. The power conferred on Special Areas Development Authorities to levy property tax is contained in section 129A and section 133 of the M.P. Municipalities Act, 1961. [24F] 2(2) The State legislature had no power to impose property tax or buildings tax on lands or buildings. The general purpose behind the declaration contained in Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act is that the Special area Development Authority shall have the powers which a Municipal Corporation or a municipal council has under the Madhya Nadu Municipalities Act. [25F] 3(3) The power to levy tax on land and buildings is not subject to the control conferred by section 129 of the State legislature on the Special Areas development Authorities to collect the property taxes. The paramount purpose behind declaration contained therein was to regulate and develop the Coal mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources. [26G] 4(4) The Act of 1957 made by Parliament alone is in any manner defeated by legitimate exercise Of taxing power by the Central Government under Section 127A and Section 135 of Municipal Corporation. The Act is in no way defeated or affected by the legislative competence of the Parliament. [27F G] 5(5) The provisions introduced by the Act of 1956 are not repugnant to the provisions contained in the Act, of 1957. The declaration made by the Parliament in respect of a declared industrial undertaking under the Industrial Development and Regulation Act, 1948 is in accordance with law. [28G H] 6(6) The impugned legislation is in contravention of the constitutional mandate contained in Article 254(1).

The appellant, a landholder of a private land, leased to the respondent for a period exceeding one year. The lease was for a term exceeding one month and the lease was not enforceable against the Government. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of termination on the ground that it had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that, as the lease had been extended beyond one year, it was not enforced against the State. The High Court held that the termination of the appellant 's leasehold rights which were created after July 1 , 1945, could only be done under the third proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The words " such right in the third Proviso" refer to the rights created before the notified date but after July I, 1945. The words 'foregoing proviso ' are not intended to be superimposed on the right of the Government to terminate the lease in favour of the petitioner. If any condition was intended to been imposed on the respondent by reason of section 20 (1) it would have expected those conditions to be mentioned in the second proviso itself. [560 D] (ii) The true meaning of the third provisos is that the words "such right" in the fourth proviso refer to rights created after the notified dates but before July 1. 1945, one would have required those conditions also to be specified in the first proviso. If the Government intended to avail itself of the right under the second Proviso it could only mean that rights created prior to the notified day but after the date notified would be enforceable against it. [561 E] (iii) The third proviso merely enables the Government, if it intends to avail themselves of the rights conferred on it by the second provisos, to terminate such rights created thereafter and in such cases compensation will be payable under section 20.(2). If any conditions were intended to have reference to the right created after January 1, 1946, one should have expected that those conditions should comply with the conditions laid down in the fifth proviso itself, void as against the government without any further necessity for any overt act to be done by the Government on or after July1, 1945 and in so far as the rights were created before July I. 1945. [562 G H] (iv) The second proviso to s.20(1), which provides that "such rights shall not be enforceable if it relates to the private land of the landholder within the meaning of section 3, clause (10), of the Estates Land Act, 1908, and such rights, created after 7 1, 1944, are only voidable at the instance of the State Government without any necessity for some overt act. The second Proviso does not contemplate that the right should be terminated or allowed to be terminated only in accordance with that proviso.
